Furthermore, previously you refuted the views regarding the two limits of arising and ceasing; now you refute the views regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
The intent of the current question is as follows:
If a practitioner of contemplation accords with the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching, when observing the arising of phenomena, which view does he cause to cease?
Regarding "extinguishing which views," this questions the intent of the Buddha’s teaching; it provisionally cites one aspect while simultaneously revealing the contemplation of extinction.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “Bodhisattva!...”
If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing dharmas arise, cause the view of non-existence to cease, and upon seeing dharmas perish, cause the view of existence to cease;
if they eliminate these views, they will attain the true non-existence of dharmas, enter the state of definitive nature, and realize definitive non-arising.
The Commentary states:

"When one sees dharmas arising" refers to correctly contemplating the time when conventional dharmas arise through causes and conditions; at this time, one is able to abandon the view that grasps at emptiness, and thus it is said that the view of non-existence is extinguished.

Regarding "seeing the time when phenomena cease": it means correctly contemplating that conventional phenomena are originally in a state of cessation; at this time, one is able to abandon views that grasp at existence, and thus it is said that "it causes the view of existence to cease."
Why is it said here that "one causes [them] to cease"?
It is because the Buddha’s teaching enables the practitioner to bring about cessation.

This meaning precisely clarifies that for one practicing contemplation, when observing the arising of phenomena, they merely depart from the view of non-existence and do not cling to arising; when observing quiescent cessation, they merely depart from the view of existence and do not grasp at cessation.
Why is this so? If one maintains the existence of birth, birth is fundamentally quiescent;
if one grasps at cessation, cessation is itself the arising of birth.
As the verse states: "The meaning of that which arises from causes and conditions is that this meaning is cessation, not arising.
The meaning of the cessation of all arising and ceasing is that this meaning is arising, not cessation.
Thus, one is able to transcend the two extremes without clinging to the middle.
If one merely abandons non-existence while grasping at existence, or destroys existence while grasping at emptiness, this is a deluded emptiness rather than true non-existence.

Now, although one has abandoned existence, one does not maintain [a fixation on] emptiness; in this way, one attains the true non-existence of all phenomena, and thus it is said that "one attains the true non-existence of dharmas."
The meaning of certainty has already been explained above.
When one attains true emptiness, the mind is observed to be non-arising; because one is far removed from all minds of existence and non-existence, it is said that there is certainly no arising.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!
To cause those sentient beings to abide in non-arising—is that itself non-arising?"
The Commentary states:
This is the fourth question and answer below.
Previously, it was explained that true contemplation is free from the characteristics of the two extremes; now, it is revealed that deluded understanding does not transcend arising and abiding.

This refers to the conceptual-linguistic discrimination (*manojalpa-vikalpa*) of a practitioner who has studied little but cultivates meditation; while contemplating that phenomena are unarisen (*anutpāda*), they are able to gather their distraction and abide in the object of non-arising, forming the thought: "This is non-arising."

Later, upon emerging from meditative concentration, he gave rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), thinking to himself that he had already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
To destroy this affliction, [the Buddha] raised it as a question, asking:
"Is abiding in the non-arising [of phenomena] itself the non-arising?"
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, "To abide in non-arising is itself arising. Why is this so?"
"Non-abiding and non-arising are themselves non-arising.
The Commentary states:
There are two parts to the answer: a brief response and a detailed elaboration.
This is a brief response consisting of two statements:
the first statement explains "arising" in accordance with the truth—that dwelling in the realm of non-arising is precisely the arising of the discriminating mind;

the second statement explains "non-arising" by way of contrast—that if the mind does not dwell [upon] the realm of non-arising and is free from all discrimination, this is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, know that there is abiding which is not the patience of non-arising; thus it is explained by way of reversal.
The brief response concludes here.
The Sūtra says: “O Bodhisattva!

If arising is non-arising, then by means of the extinction of arising, both arising and extinction are extinguished together. Fundamental arising is non-arising; the mind is eternally empty and quiescent. Being empty and quiescent, it has no abiding; that the mind has no abiding is precisely non-arising.
The Commentary says:
This is a further detailed examination.
Within it, there are two parts:
First, examine arising; subsequently, examine non-arising.

If one dwells within the mind of arising and gives rise to the realm of non-arising, this is precisely using arising to extinguish the arising of that realm; therefore, it is said that if one gives rise to non-arising, one uses arising to extinguish arising.

Although the arising of objects is extinguished, one grasps at the non-existence of that extinction; since a mind capable of grasping arises within the non-existent state of those objects, both arising and extinction coexist—how, then, can this be called "non-arising"?
These two phrases, as explained previously, refer to arising.

True patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is not like this: externally there is no persistence of the grasped object (*grāhya*), and internally there is no production of the grasping subject (*grāhaka*). For this reason, it is said that both arising and ceasing are extinguished.

However, this simultaneous cessation does not mean returning to non-existence. When one investigates its original birth, that birth cannot be found; since its birth cannot be found, how can there be a return to cessation?
At that moment, one realizes that it is originally empty and quiescent; therefore, it is said that its original birth is non-birth and the mind is eternally empty and quiescent.

Thus, in this emptiness and stillness where subject and object are equal, there is no abiding mind that dwells within the realm of emptiness; therefore, it is said that "emptiness and stillness are non-abiding.
This is precisely what is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); hence, it is said to be "non-arising."
The exposition of the contemplation of non-arising has already been concluded above.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Venerable One!..."
If the mind has no abiding, what is there to cultivate and study?
Is it for those in training (śaikṣa),
or for those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
The Commentary states:
From here below, the meaning of a single awakening is explained in detail.
Within this section, there are eight question-and-answer exchanges, which are divided into two parts:

The first two questions and answers correctly and extensively expound the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as a single awakening; the subsequent six questions and answers, arising from the discussion, resolve various doubts and difficulties.

Now, regarding this first question, it asks whether the mind abides nowhere: if one is a practitioner in training (*śaikṣa*), then there is no non-abiding; if one is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), then there is no contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, if there were those still in training (*śaikṣa*), they would have to possess a mind that arises; if there were those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they would be nothing but the principle of emptiness.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “O Bodhisattva!...”
"The mind of non-arising has no coming or going; its fundamental nature as the *tathāgatagarbha* is quiescent and immovable.
The Commentary states:
Herein, the principle is first revealed, followed by a direct response to the question.

As for manifesting the principle: one attains the state of non-abiding; with a mind that is unborn, the mind is constantly quiescent and never emerges from contemplation. Realizing that there is originally no arising and that there is no beginning entry, for this reason it is said that the mind has neither entering nor exiting.

When one observes the mind in this way and finds it has neither entry nor exit, this is precisely the originally awakened *tathāgatagarbha*-mind; it clarifies that initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) is identical to original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
Since this unborn mind is the fundamental treasury, its nature is primordially quiescent and no longer gives rise to movement; how, then, could there be entry, exit, arising, or ceasing?
This statement further establishes the meaning of being without entering or exiting.

The Sūtra says: “It is neither that of one in training (śaikṣa) nor that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). There is no training or non-training; this is what constitutes being beyond training. It is not that there is no training, for therein lies that which is to be trained.”
The Commentary says:
This is the direct response to the meaning of the question.
Within it, there are two parts:
First there is negation, and later there is affirmation.
Since it is not an initial entry, it is not that of one in training (śaikṣa);
since there is no final exit, it is not that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, because there is no mind that abides, it is not "with training" (śaikṣa);
because it is not the case that there is no mind that does not abide, it is not "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
This is a double negation, a phrase of exclusion.

That there is neither one in training nor one beyond training is precisely what constitutes being "beyond training" (aśaikṣa); because there is no distinct object to be learned, there is no corresponding subject who learns. For this reason, it is accepted as being beyond training.
This is based on the meaning of "not being a learner" (*aśaikṣa*) that it is permitted to be "one beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

It is not that there is no learning which constitutes what is to be learned; although it is not the contemplation of abiding, it is not without the practice of non-abiding. For this reason, it is permitted to be a "learner" (*śaikṣa*).

Since there is that which is still to be learned, the training pertaining to the lower stages is "with-learner" (*śaikṣa*) by virtue of this meaning of not being "beyond-learning" (*aśaikṣa*); thus it is accepted as being with-learner.
This is a response given with full autonomy, based on mutual acceptance.
The sutra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Why is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha quiescent and immovable?"
The Commentary states:
This is the second section of questions and answers below.

Previously, it was clarified that initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) is not different from the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; now, the text correctly reveals that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains hidden and unmoving.
Herein, the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* is briefly elucidated.
There are two or three gateways to the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Regarding the threefold classification, as stated in the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra*: "Within the realm of sentient beings, three kinds of dharmas are shown; all are true suchness (*tathatā*), neither different nor distinct."
What are the three dharmas?

First is the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha that accords with the primordial limit and its pure dharmas; these dharmas are as they truly are, non-false, neither separate nor detached from inconceivable wisdom, and this essence of the pure corresponding dharma has existed since the beginningless primordial limit.

Second, the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally dissociated from the impure dharmas that constitute the entanglements of afflictions; this fundamental dissociation from the impure dharmas of the entanglements of afflictions can only be severed by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of awakening.

Third, the Tathāgatagarbha is equal and eternal throughout the future limit and is the existent reality; it is the root of all dharmas, encompassing all dharmas and possessing all dharmas, never departing from nor separated from worldly phenomena.
The commentary states:
This reveals three gateways to the *tathāgatagarbha*.
What are these three?
First, it can encompass the Tathāgatagarbha; when abiding in its own nature, it can encompass the merits of the Tathāgata at the stage of fruition.
It is called the Tathāgatagarbha because it is able to encompass the Tathāgata.

Second is the Tathāgatagarbha as that which is encompassed: this refers to the impure phenomena enshrouded by afflictions, all of which exist within the wisdom of the Tathāgata and are entirely sustained by the Tathāgata.
That which is encompassed by the Tathāgata is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Third, the concealment of the *tathāgatagarbha* refers to the fact that the *dharmakāya*-Tathāgata is shrouded by afflictions;
because the Tathāgata is thus concealed, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha spoke thus.
To explain his text:
when it says that the equality of the future limit is constant and existent, it means that the essence of the one mind pervades the three time periods.
However, since the prior two gates have already revealed the limit of the beginning (*pūrvakoṭi*), this gate clarifies the limit of the future (*aparānta*) and so forth.
Furthermore, it seeks to reveal the meaning of "Tathāgata": that which is equal and constant throughout the limit of the future is precisely the meaning of "Thus" (*tathā*).
To speak of "existence" refers to its coming-to-be. As the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"This True Suchness (tathatā) is not such that there is 'suchness' within it; even that which is not suchness is likewise suchness."
The "suchness" (tathatā) of the two vehicles is the suchness within that which is not-suchness; there is no non-suchness within that which is not-suchness. Why is this so?

Because those of the two vehicles take the marks of impermanence and so forth—observed through false conceptualization—as true suchness. This false conceptualization exists only on the causal stage and is absent on the stage of fruition; therefore, this suchness of theirs is subject to either formation or destruction.

The suchness of a bodhisattva is free from falsehood; by observing suchness in accordance with true nature, there is no difference between cause and effect, for it is only perfected and never destroyed.
Thus it is said, and so forth at length.
Therefore, we know that the "equality and constancy of the posterior limit" precisely reveals the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) in the Mahāyāna.
As for the statement regarding the meaning of "the arrival of clarity," this clarifies the coming of the one mind in contrast to the departure of ordinary phenomena.
Just as when an ordinary person departs, the phenomena of the five aggregates of clinging do not reach the stage of fruition; they depart and do not return.
This suchness of the one mind remains even at the stage of fruition and never passes away; therefore, the statement "reaching existence" (*yāvad asti*) reveals the meaning of "returning."
As the treatise states, "From abiding in its own nature to the attainment [of realization]," this refers precisely to this point.

Thus, because this single mind universally serves as the locus of support for all defiled and pure phenomena, it is the fundamental source of all dharmas and the gate of primordial stillness; since it is not lacking in any of the sands-of-the-Ganges virtues, it is said to "encompass all dharmas.
Furthermore, because the gate of movement according to conditions is not lacking in any of the sands-of-the-Ganges defiled dharmas, it is said to "possess all dharmas."

However, if one takes defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) as the standard to measure the essence of mind (*citta-tattva*), they cannot be said to pervade it universally; therefore, [the essence] is "detached" from them.

Conversely, if one takes the essence of mind as the standard to measure all defiled phenomena, it pervades all such phenomena without anything being beyond its reach; thus, it is said that within worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*), it is neither "separate" nor "detached. This meaning of being neither separate nor detached is the meaning of being "concealed" (*gūḍha*).
This third gate generally clarifies that the single mind serves as the basis for both defilement and purity throughout both movement and stillness;
the second gate specifically reveals the gate of movement as the basis for defiled phenomena;
and the first gate specifically reveals the gate of stillness as the basis for pure phenomena.

Regarding the second point, the statement "the essence that is dissociated from the primordial limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*) means that all afflictive phenomena are termed "dissociated" because they contradict the essence of the mind. Since the essence of the single mind serves as the basis for those [afflictions] by functioning as the gate of movement in accordance with conditions, it is therefore the essence of the dissociated phenomena.

Regarding the mention of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and the impure dharmas: they function in dependence upon the dharma and the essence of the mind, causing the essence of one's own mind to follow along with defilement. Therefore, by taking both the dependent and the supported dharmas together, they constitute the second essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Only that which can be severed by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom is so severed; for it is only the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that can correctly sever it.
This point is explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Two Obstructions" (*dvaya-āvaraṇa-pariccheda*).

Regarding the first point, the "essence associated with the primordial limit" (pūrvakoṭi-saṃprayukta-svabhāva): it is the essence of associated merit because it is inherently associated with the mind, possessing virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the gate of primordial quiescence.

Regarding what is called the "pure dharma," because its nature as a basis for qualities is free from defilement, one takes both the basis and that which depends upon it together as the primary essence of the Tathāgatagarbha.

This teaching—which is as it truly is, non-illusory, inseparable, and not detached from inconceivable wisdom—explains the meaning of "correspondence" (*yoga*), because this meaning of the *dharmakāya* corresponds with all qualities of merit (*guṇadharma*).
As stated above:
"That which is non-separate, non-detached, uninterrupted, non-different, and in accord with the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas is called the Dharma-body.
What is the meaning of this?
This essence of the single mind briefly possesses five characteristics. What are these five?

First, it is far removed from the differentiated characteristics of the grasped object; second, it is liberated from the conceptual clinging of the grasping subject; third, it is universally equal throughout the three limits of time; fourth, it is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception; and fifth, it does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence, oneness or difference, transcending the sphere of mental activity and surpassing the path of language.
The original merits that exceed the sands of the Ganges also possess five meanings that correspond to its essence:

first, because each individual merit is free from the characteristics of the apprehended object (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*), it is not something apart from the Dharma-body; thus it corresponds with the first characteristic, as the Sūtra says, "not separate."

Second, because each and every merit is liberated from the grasping of the grasper (*grāhaka*), it is not that which is liberated by the Dharma-body; rather, it corresponds with the second characteristic, as the sutra states: "not liberated."

Third, each and every one of these virtues extends throughout the limits of the three periods of time; even if there were no prior or subsequent limits, they would not be severed, for they correspond with the third characteristic, and thus are said to be "uninterrupted.

Fourth, each and every one of these virtues is equal to the realm of empty space; horizontally, there is no distinction between this or that location, for they correspond with the fourth characteristic, and thus are said to be "undifferentiated."

Fifth, each and every merit is free from all extremes; it is not an object of discursive thought and transcends the path of language, corresponding to the fifth characteristic, as the sutra says, "inconceivable."

All dharmas of merit possess these five meanings; they are non-different from their essence and are integrated into a single flavor. By this principle, they are called "conjoined" (*saṃprayukta*), which is not like the conjoining of a king with his attendants as distinct entities.

Now, regarding the statement herein that "it is not separate from nor detached from the inconceivable dharma of wisdom," this briefly cites the meaning of awakening among all merits and briefly explains three meanings within the fivefold correspondence; this is the first treasury of inclusion.
The meaning of the three kinds of treasuries has been briefly described as such.
Regarding the two gates, as stated in the *Bhāryāsūtra*: "The empty tathāgatagarbha is that which is separated from, liberated from, or distinct from all the storehouses of afflictions;
the non-empty tathāgatagarbha is that which is not separated from, not liberated from, and not distinct from the inconceivable buddhadharmas."

The commentary states: All afflictive phenomena are false and deceptive; they are "false" (*śūnya*) because their objects are unreal, and "deceptive" (*mṛṣā*) because their nature is distracted. Being deceptive, they lack truth; being false, they lack reality. Because they lack true reality, they are called "empty. That which can conceal the Tathāgata is named the *tathāgatagarbha*; this is precisely the meaning of emptiness, as it obscures and covers the Truth.
The unreal characteristics of the objects of all afflictions are what the *dharmakāya* is free from; therefore, it is said "if free.
The bonds of false attachment that constitute the essence of all afflictions are what the *dharmakāya* has shed; therefore, it is said "if shed."
To say they are different would mean that the aforementioned false, differentiated conceptualizations would contradict the equality of the Dharmakāya.
Because these three meanings are thus inconsistent, there is no reality; this is precisely the meaning of emptiness.

Regarding the term "not empty": all merits are in correspondence with its essence. Because the essence is not false, it is "true"; because the object is not void, it is "real. Due to this reality, it is called "not empty."

The phrase "the Tathāgata is covered over" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*; the subsequent phrases such as "not separate" and "not detached" explain the meaning of its being non-empty, the significance of which has already been explained under the three types of *garbha* gates.

However, herein, the essence of the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is the first of the three aforementioned dharmas; the meaning of "emptiness" therein is the second; and the meaning of being "concealed" among those three types of Tathāgatagarbha is combined in the third. Thus, while the former two [dharmas] separately manifest the two meanings of the "grasper" and the "grasped," these present two gates of Tathāgatagarbha—intending to manifest the meaning of emptiness and the concealment of reality—separately manifest the two meanings of the "concealer" and the "concealed."
Furthermore, these two sūtras mutually clarify distinct meanings; this is why they are explained differently through the two gates.
Let us now set aside the discussion on the vehicles and return to explaining the main text.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said:
"The Tathāgatagarbha possesses the characteristics of arising, ceasing, deliberation, and cognition.
When its underlying principle is obscured and not manifested, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; its nature is quiescent and immovable.
The Commentary states:
The characteristic of the cognition that arises and ceases is precisely the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
However, in this passage, the capacity is made manifest while the meaning is concealed; thus, it is not explicitly designated as the *tathāgatagarbha*.
To say that the principle is concealed and not manifest is the Tathāgatagarbha;
this refers to the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, which is termed "Tathāgatagarbha" in reference to the sense of what is concealed.
To say that its nature is quiescent and immovable reveals that although this nature of the Garbha is concealed, it remains unchanged.
This nature (*svabhāva*) has five meanings, as explained in the *Nirākāra-śāstra*.
First, the meaning of "category" is the meaning of "nature.

For example, all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), such as jars and garments, do not depart from the category of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); they all take the four great elements as their nature.
Thus, these sentient beings do not emerge from a single realm, as they all take that single realm as their generic category (*jāti*).

What is termed "generic category" (*jāti*) in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) in the *Buddhadhātuśāstra*; while the terminology differs, the underlying meaning is no different.
Second, the meaning of "cause" (hetu) is the meaning of "nature" (prakṛti).
For example, fire exists within wood as its nature; because it acts as the cause for fire, it is called "nature.
Likewise, the various untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma) of the noble ones are accomplished by taking this as their cause.
In those two treatises, this refers to the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
Third, the meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*) is the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*).
For example, when refined gold gives rise to an ornamental object, the arising of that ornament has gold as its nature.
This realm is likewise so: it can give rise to the fivefold Dharma-body of the stage of fruition, and the arising of this Dharma-body takes this realm as its nature.
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is also termed the "meaning of arising";

in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it is termed the "meaning of attainment. Since the meaning of the cause exists prior to the fruition, [the term] is applied to what has already arisen and is thus called the "meaning of attainment."
Fourth, the meaning of being unchanging is the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*).

Just as the nature of a diamond jewel remains for an eon without increase or decrease, so too does this realm remain equal throughout the three periods of time; the mundane is indestructible and the supramundane is inexhaustible.
In those two treatises, it is called the "meaning of reality" (*tattvārtha*); "reality" means that which is indestructible, and thus while the terminology differs, the intent is the same.
Fifth, the meaning of the "esoteric treasury" (*guhyakośa*) is the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*).

Just as there is the nature of true gold within yellow stone, yet it provides no benefit unless the ore is broken open; once it is processed through refinement, it possesses the utility of a treasure—therefore, that nature has the sense of being hidden.

One should know that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is likewise: when its envelopments are not destroyed, it is external and defiled; when the destruction of the envelopments is attained, it becomes internal and pure. Therefore, one knows that this nature has the meaning of a secret treasury.

In the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it is termed "the meaning of secrecy" (*guhyārtha*); in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is termed "the meaning of treasury" (*kośārtha*). It is clearly evident that the meanings are identical while the terminology differs.

In this present text, the term "nature" (*dhātu*) encompasses these five meanings; the phrase "tranquil and immovable" briefly reveals the latter two, for "tranquil" signifies the meaning of the secret treasury and "immovable" signifies the meaning of being unchanging.
The detailed exposition of the meaning of the single awakening is hereby concluded.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Venerable One!”
"What is the characteristic of the discerning cognition of arising and ceasing?
The Treatise says:
From this point forward, there are six questions and answers; based on these discussions, further points are raised to resolve various doubts and difficulties.
This question and answer clarify the characteristics of being able to conceal one's deliberations while knowing [the truth].
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “Bodhisattva!...”
"It is logically impossible for there not to be [this].
If there were 'yes' or 'no,' then various thoughts would immediately arise; these thousand reflections and myriad deliberations are the marks of arising and ceasing.
The Treatise says:
This response consists of two layers: first, a brief answer, followed by a detailed exposition.
Within the brief section, there are two sentences:
first, the object of delusion is presented.
The principle that causes delusion is where the movements of the mind cease; therefore, it is said that the principle is "neither existent nor non-existent.
"Existent" (ke) means "is," and "non-existent" (bu) means "is not.
The principle transcends the four propositions and is free from all right and wrong; it is not a domain traversed by the discriminating mind.
Next, the deluding agent is revealed.

If there were "yes" or "no," thoughts would immediately arise; because there is ignorance (*avidyā*) that fails to perceive equality, there is the discriminating mind of "yes" and "no. From this, the six types of defiled minds are fully generated.

Regarding the statement that "thousands of thoughts and myriad deliberations are the marks of arising and ceasing": although the six types of defiled minds vary in their coarseness or subtlety, they all contradict equanimity and are therefore marks of arising and ceasing. As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Furthermore, to distinguish the marks of arising and ceasing, there are briefly two kinds."
What are the two?
First is the coarse, because it is associated with the mind;
second is the subtle, because it is dissociated from the mind.
Furthermore, that which is coarse among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings;
that which is subtle among the coarse and coarse among the subtle is the realm of bodhisattvas;
and that which is subtle among the subtle is the realm of Buddhas.

These two kinds of arising and ceasing exist based upon the perfuming of ignorance; that is to say, they depend upon causes and they depend upon conditions. Dependence upon causes refers to the meaning of non-awakening, while dependence upon conditions refers to the meaning of the false construction of objective realms.
"If the cause ceases, then the condition ceases; because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases, and because the condition ceases, the associated mind ceases.
According to the commentary:
"The 'coarse' factors here that are associated with the mind refer to the three kinds of defilements associated with the mind."
That which is subtle and non-associated with the mind refers to the three types of non-associated defilements (*asamprayukta-kleśa*).

That which is coarse among the coarse refers to the defilement associated with grasping (*grāha-samprayukta-kleśa*) and the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anuccheda-samprayukta-kleśa*); as both reside within the six consciousnesses, they belong to the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The subtle among the coarse refers to the defilement associated with discriminative cognition, which resides in the seventh consciousness.
The coarse among the subtle refers to the defilement dissociated from manifested form and the defilement dissociated from the perceiving mind.
The subtlest among the subtle refers to the defilements that are dissociated from the fundamental karma.
These three all reside within the state of the eighth consciousness.
Regarding these three types of subtle arising and ceasing, they are moved by the wind of ignorance; therefore, it is said that because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases.
Among these, the three kinds of coarse arising and ceasing are moved by the winds of objective conditions; therefore, it is said that because the conditions cease, the corresponding mind ceases.
The details therein are as explained in the commentary on that treatise.
The "thousand thoughts" mentioned in this sutra collectively encompass all non-associated (viprayukta) defiled subtle discriminations;
the "ten thousand considerations" collectively encompass all associated (samprayukta) defiled mental coarse discriminations.
Both of these are manifestations of shifting thoughts; for this reason, they are said to be the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
The Sūtra says: "O Bodhisattva!

Contemplate the principle of the original nature, which is inherently complete. A thousand reflections and ten thousand deliberations do not benefit the Way; they merely cause agitation and disturbance, causing one to lose the sovereign mind."
The commentary states:
What follows is an extensive exposition.
This consists of three parts:

First, the fulfillment of the principle is revealed in contrast to the characteristics of arising and ceasing; second, the defects of defilement are clarified in contrast to the fulfillment of the principle; third, the benefit of following the principle to extinguish defilement, abandon movement, and proceed toward tranquility is distinguished.
The term "bodhisattva" mentioned at the beginning refers to the appellation for a bodhisattva who has attained liberation.
Regarding the phrase "observing the fundamental nature and characteristics," it means that the Buddha observes the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature.
"Self-sufficient by its very principle" means that the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the object of contemplation, is replete with immeasurable qualities of nature.

As the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "Furthermore, regarding the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*): from the very beginning, its nature is spontaneously complete with all merits. That is to say, its essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light; the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm; the meaning of true and authentic cognition; the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind; the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty."

Because it is fully endowed with such inconceivable Buddha-dharmas—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—which are inseparable, uninterrupted, and non-different, and because it is fulfilled in every sense without any deficiency, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and also the *tathāgatakāya*.
Now, the principle of this sutra is inherently complete, as it collectively manifests the perfection of such merits.
This concludes the first section.

Next, the faults of arising, ceasing, and the movement of thought are explained; herein, it is generally shown that these are beneficial in no way but rather cause harm. As that treatise extensively explains this meaning: "Question:"

Question: It was stated above that True Suchness (tathatā) is equal in its essence and free from all marks; why, then, is it further said that its essence possesses these various kinds of meritorious qualities? Answer:
Although these meanings of various meritorious qualities truly exist, they lack any mark of differentiation; they are identical in their single flavor, being solely True Suchness.
What is the meaning of this?
Because it is non-conceptual and free from the marks of conceptualization, it is non-dual.
Furthermore, by what principle can one speak of its distinctions?
This is shown by means of the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the *karmic consciousness*. How is this shown?

Because all phenomena are fundamentally mind-only and truly devoid of marks or conceptualization, yet there is a deluded mind that, through non-awakening, gives rise to thoughts and perceives various objective realms; therefore, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*). When the nature of the mind does not arise, this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.
If the mind gives rise to views, there is immediately the characteristic of non-seeing;
for the nature of the mind is free from views, which is precisely the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.

If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition; it lacks self-nature, and is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure, even to the extent of being fully possessed of deluded and defiled meanings exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding this meaning, it is shown that when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of all pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
if the mind were to arise and perceive any further phenomena as objects of recollection, it would be deficient.
Such immeasurable merits of pure dharmas are themselves the single mind, with nothing further to be contemplated; therefore, being fully perfected, it is called the Tathāgata-garbha, the Dharma-body.

Regarding the statement in this sutra that [the mind] is merely a source of agitation and disturbance: because the mind undergoes movement, it is not true cognition; since it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is devoid of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is said to be "agitated."
Because views arise from the mind, there are such things as the aspect of non-seeing; therefore, it is called "confusion.
As for "losing the sovereign of the original mind": immeasurable merit is precisely the one mind, and because this one mind is the ruler, it is named the "mind-sovereign" (citta-rāja).
Arising, ceasing, and turbulent movement cause one to deviate from this mind-king so that it cannot return; therefore, it is said that [the mind] is lost.

The Sūtra says: "If there is no thought or deliberation, then there is no arising or ceasing. When things do not arise according to reality, the various consciousnesses are peaceful and still, their continuous flow does not arise, and one attains the purity of the five dharmas—this is called the Mahāyāna."
The Commentary states:
The following third section concerns the process of extinguishing defilements in accordance with principle, departing from movement and proceeding toward tranquility.
Within this, there are two parts:
This clearly reveals and reaffirms that one leaves movement and proceeds toward quiescence. For one who is free from discursive thought,
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the stage of Buddhahood, they gradually accord with the single-minded, equal Dharma-realm, because all discursive thought and discrimination are forever absent.

Regarding "that which is without arising and ceasing": previously, due to discursive thought, there were the characteristics of arising and ceasing; now, because there is no discursive thought and there is forever no differentiation, one is ultimately free from both types of arising and ceasing.

From this point forward, one accords with principle and remains unmoving; reaching the end of the future, one never again returns to movement. Therefore, it is said that "according to reality, there is no arising.

When the two kinds of arising and ceasing are ultimately stilled, the movements of the eight consciousnesses all return to stillness, and the six defiled flows are forever extinguished and do not arise. Therefore, it is said that "all consciousnesses are peaceful and silent, and their flows do not arise."

Because the continuous flow [of consciousness] does not arise, the Dharma-realm is perfectly revealed; because all cognitions are settled in tranquility, the four wisdoms are fully accomplished. Thus it is said that one attains the purity of the five dharmas.
No function of transport and support surpasses this; therefore, the conclusion states: "This is called the Mahāyāna."
The section clarifying the movement toward stillness is now complete.
The Sūtra says: “O Bodhisattva!

When one enters the five dharmas that purify the mind, there is no delusion. If there is no delusion, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s noble self-realized wisdom. One who enters this stage of wisdom thoroughly knows that all things are unborn from the very beginning; knowing they are unborn from the beginning, one is free from conceptual construction.”
The Commentary states:
This is a further elucidation consisting of three phrases.

First, regarding the statement that "entering the purity of the five dharmas means the mind is without delusion": when one returns to the source of the mind, there is no longer the non-awakening of deluded thought.

The second statement—that if there is no delusion, one immediately enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realized noble wisdom—is because upon the exhaustion of non-awakening, one immediately enters the stage of the perfect wisdom of initial awakening; thus, it reveals the fulfillment of initial awakening in contrast to non-awakening.

Regarding the third entry into the stage of wisdom: it refers to skillfully knowing that all things are fundamentally unborn, and knowing that fundamental non-arising is itself the absence of deluded thought. When initial enlightenment (śikṣābodha) is fulfilled, one is able to know that the four marks of non-enlightenment (aśikṣābodha)—the movement of thought—have been fundamentally unborn from the beginning; thus, one knows that there has fundamentally been no deluded thought. This demonstrates that initial enlightenment is not different from original enlightenment (mūlabodhi).

As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All sentient beings are not called awakened because, from the very beginning, their thoughts have continued in succession without ever being free from discursive thought; therefore, it is said that they possess beginningless ignorance."
If one attains non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*), one immediately knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the marks of the mind.

Because of this equality of non-conceptualization, there is in reality no distinction between initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*) and subsequent enlightenment; for the four marks exist simultaneously, none of which possess independent self-existence, being originally equal and identical with awakening.
The commentary states:

Herein, the statement that "if one attains non-thought (amṛta), one immediately knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of mental characteristics" reveals that, within the sutra, this constitutes thorough knowledge of all things.
That "in reality there is no distinction of initial awakening" (ādi-bodha) reveals that, according to the Sūtra, one thoroughly knows that [the mind] is from the beginning unborn (*an-utpanna*).

That "the four marks exist simultaneously and all lack self-establishment, being originally equal and identical with single awakening" reveals that, according to the Sūtra, knowing the original non-arising is itself the absence of deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
The analogy of crossing a river in a dream should be explained here in detail.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying, “Venerable One!
"One who is without conceptual construction should have no cessation.
The Commentary states:
From here below is the second question and answer, clarifying that there is no cessation.
The meaning of the question is as follows:

If there were originally no deluded thoughts, then there would be nothing to cease. Since there is nothing to cease, that which ceases is also non-existent. Since that which ceases does not exist, there should likewise be no initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).
Such is the objection.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “O Bodhisattva!”
Delusion is fundamentally unarisen; there is no delusion that can be extinguished.
Knowing that the mind is mindless, there is no mind that can be stilled.
Without division or distinction, the manifesting consciousness does not arise; that there is no arising to be stilled is itself neither cessation nor non-cessation.
"Why is this? Because cessation itself has no cessation.
The Treatise says:
The meaning of the response is twofold: first, it grants that there is no cessation; second, it negates that there is no cessation.
The grant is because initial enlightenment is not different from original enlightenment.
The negation is because initial enlightenment is not solely original enlightenment.
If one asks what the difference is between "allowing [the mind] to rest" (xi) and "stopping" (zhi):

[the former] refers to resting because of the movement of delusions, and [the latter] refers to stopping because the mind is distracted; yet, since there is fundamentally no arising and no distraction, there is nothing that can be rested or stopped.
"Without division" means that there is no objective aspect distinct from the seeing.
"Without distinction" means that there is no seeing distinct from the objective aspect.
Since the objective aspect and the seeing are already without differentiation, the manifesting consciousness is fundamentally non-arising.
The non-arising of the past and future is known by both the ignorant and the wise.

With respect to the present, one clarifies primordial non-arising (*mūla-anutpāda*); since there is no arising of non-awakening that could be ceased, there is likewise no distinction of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) as that which could effect such cessation.
This is accepted according to the perspective of non-differentiation.
Nor is it that there is no cessation, for there is no beginningless awakening that is not non-differentiated.
As for "cessation through the absence of cessation," it means that the deluded mind, which is unarisen, is brought to rest.
Although arising cannot be apprehended, it is not merely the case that there is no arising.
Because it is not merely the case that there is no arising, it is not that there is nothing upon which to rest; therefore, it is not that there is no awakening capable of resting therein.
The answer was as follows.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"If cessation is itself non-cessation, then cessation is precisely arising; what, then, is meant by 'non-arising'?
The Commentary states:
From here below is the third question and answer, which elucidates the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The intent of the objection is as follows:
If there is an awakening capable of ceasing [ignorance], then there arises an insight capable of ceasing it;
thus, although the arising of non-awakening is dispelled, the arising of initial awakening still persists.
What is meant by "the contemplation that realizes non-arising"?
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “O Bodhisattva!...”
"When this arising ceases, having ceased, there is no cessation; it neither dwells in non-cessation nor dwells in non-dwelling. How, then, can this be 'arising'?
The commentary states:
The answer has two aspects—first granting [the premise], and then refuting it.
"Granting" refers to the permission granted during the preparatory contemplation (*upāya-bhāvanā*) that enables one to cease the arising of the mind.

For example, at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), although the arising of consciousness is ceased, one does not grasp at that consciousness; rather, one is able to cease the mind's grasping and cause non-arising to manifest.
When this cessation occurs, it is precisely that which is called arising; for this reason, it is said that "when ceasing, there is arising.

Once this single moment has passed, one does not grasp at non-existence. Because one does not grasp at non-existence, the grasping mind does not arise; for this reason, it is said that "once ceased, there is no further cessation."

At this time, because one is far removed from all conceptual discrimination, one does not abide in a non-abiding non-existence, nor does one grasp at the self-nature of that non-abiding mind; subject and object are forever severed, in a state of absolute equality.
"How can this birth be obtained at such a time?
Thus he answered.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable One!
What is there to be taken up or discarded regarding the mind of non-arising?
In what dharma-characteristic does it abide?”
The Buddha said:
“The mind of non-arising neither grasps nor abandons; it abides in no-mind and abides in no-dharma.
The Commentary says:
This is the fourth question-and-answer session, which dispels the views of superimposition and denial.

It refers to the thought held by those in training (*śaikṣa*) that the mind entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) grasps the principle of signlessness (*animitta*) while abandoning all phenomena characterized by signs (*nimitta*).
To dispel this view of superimposition, it is said that one neither grasps nor rejects.
Alternatively, one might think:

at the time of entering meditative observation, there is no dharma whatsoever upon which to abide, nor is there a mind capable of abiding; thus, this is not different from ultimate unconditionedness (*atyanta-asamskrta*).
To eliminate this view of negation, it is said that one "dwells in non-mind" and "dwells in non-dharmas.
Although there is no dwelling, it is not that there is no dwelling; because it is not a case of no dwelling, one can say that one dwells.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does one dwell in non-mind and dwell in non-dharmas?"
The Buddha said:
"That which does not arise in the mind is dwelling in non-mind; that which does not arise in phenomena is dwelling in non-phenomena.
The Commentary says:
The following is the fifth section of questions and answers, which further dispels lingering doubts.
Regarding the phrase "lingering doubt":
since it is said that [the mind] "abides," it must therefore be both the mind and a dharma.
If it is not a mental dharma, then one should say that it does not abide.
This statement is extremely profound; how can one believe and understand it?
Such is the doubt.
The Buddha’s intended meaning in his reply is as follows:

because he does not maintain the existence of the observing mind that realizes, nor the existence of the realized principle-dharma, he says it is "not produced in the mind" and "not produced in dharmas."
"Arising" implies that [the mind] still exists.

Since the mental factors (cittadharma) do not constantly exist, it is not the case that they exist through occasional non-loss of mindfulness; therefore, it is said that this is abiding in non-mind and abiding in non-dharmas.
"Abiding" (sthiti) means constancy.
Because it does not regress or fall away, it is called "abiding.
Such is the meaning of abiding.
Since they are perfectly in accord and not at odds, how could there be any contradiction between them?
This is the correct answer;
what follows is a further clarification.
The Sūtra says: “Good son!

When the dharmas of the mind do not arise, there is no basis for support and no dwelling in conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*). The mind is eternally empty and quiescent, devoid of any marks of differentiation; it is like space, which has neither movement nor stillness, neither arising nor activity, and neither ‘that’ nor ‘this.’”
"One attains the eye of the emptiness of mind and the body of the emptiness of phenomena; the five aggregates and the six sense bases are all entirely empty and quiescent.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the second layer of manifestation.
Within this, there are two parts:

first, the manifestation of being free from all signs and pervading the three periods of time; second, the manifestation of conforming to the *dharmadhātu* and fully practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Regarding the first part, there are three phrases: namely, the teaching (*dharma*), the simile (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*yoga*).
"Non-arising mental phenomena" restates the preceding main answer.
"That is, there is no basis of reliance" means that, horizontally, there is no distinction between the supporting subject and the supported object.
"Not abiding in any activities" means that, vertically, there are no past, future, or present activities.
Because there is neither past nor future, the mind is eternally empty and quiescent; because there is neither subject nor object, there are no differentiated characteristics.
The passage beginning with "It is like that" constitutes the second citation of a simile.

Regarding "there is no moving or abiding": just as the world’s space is unconditioned and eternally abiding, it lacks the movement of prior cessation and subsequent arising, serving as a metaphor for the non-abiding nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, there is no abiding of either that which depends or that upon which it depends; this is equivalent to being without any support.
Without arising and without activity, it is identical to the mind’s eternal emptiness and stillness.
There is neither "that" nor "this," and it is not different from, nor possesses any characteristic of difference.
Therefore, the analogy of empty space is raised to illustrate the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding the statement in the "Correspondence" (*he*) that one "attains the eye of the empty mind," this is because through non-arising one is able to contemplate the mind, thereby attaining the capacity to contemplate everything without exception.
Regarding "attaining the body of the emptiness of dharmas": this is because, by not giving rise to the dharmas that are observed, one attains the equal dharma-body (*samatā-dharmakāya*).

Regarding "the five aggregates are all empty": this is because, having attained the eye of the emptiness of mind, one penetrates the emptiness of the five aggregates throughout the three periods of time; this accords with the previous point regarding the non-arising and non-activity of space.

Regarding the statement that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are entirely empty: because one has attained the body of dharma-emptiness, which pervades the emptiness of the internal and external six sense bases, this accords with the preceding point that space is without "this" or "that."
The Sūtra says: “Good son!

One who cultivates the dharma of emptiness does not rely on the triple world, does not dwell upon the marks of precepts, is pure and free from discursive thought, neither grasping nor rejecting, possesses a nature equal to a vajra, does not destroy the Triple Gem, remains unmoving within the empty mind, and is endowed with the six pāramitās.”
The Commentary states:
This second section reveals the complete cultivation of the six perfections.
The phrase "one who cultivates the dharma of emptiness" reiterates the previously mentioned mind of empty quiescence.
The following section specifically elucidates the possession of the six perfections: because one does not rely on the three realms, one possesses the perfection of giving;

because one does not dwell in the characteristics of precepts, one possesses the perfection of morality; because one is pure and free from conceptualization, one possesses the perfection of patience; because there is neither grasping nor abandoning, one possesses the perfection of diligence; because one’s nature is like a vajra, one possesses the perfection of meditative concentration; and because one does not destroy the Three Jewels, one possesses the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Because the single contemplation of the mind, which universally illuminates and serves as the standard for practice, transcends all disputes; thus, it fully embodies the Three Jewels. Since the meaning of the Three Jewels is established, one’s words are indestructible.
Because the single empty mind is devoid of separate activity yet possesses the six perfections, it is said that the empty mind, being unmoving, is endowed with the six pāramitās.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Vimukta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One!..."
“The six pāramitās all possess marks; can a dharma that possesses marks transcend the world?
The Buddha said, “Good son!...”
"The six pāramitās that I have taught are signless and unconditioned.
The Commentary says:
From here below, the sixth question and answer further elucidates the meaning of the supramundane six perfections.

The questioner raises doubts, which are then resolved; thus, by citing the phenomena of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) within the mundane world, it is shown that the supramundane mind likewise possesses these six.
The response consists of two parts:
first, a brief indication; second, a detailed explanation.
This is a brief indication.
It is called "signless" because it is free from the signs of the three wheels, such as the giver, the recipient, and the gift.
It is called "unconditioned" because it is free from the three characteristics of the conditioned, such as arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Regarding what I previously stated—that a single mind possesses the six [perfections]—each and every one of them is signless and unconditioned; therefore, these six perfections are supramundane, unlike the mundane which possess signs and are conditioned.
The Sūtra says: "For what reason?

Because one skillfully enters into detachment from desire, the mind is constantly pure, and through truthful speech and skillful means, one benefits others with fundamental benefit—this is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)."
The Commentary says:
Hereafter follows the detailed explanation.
This consists of two parts:
First there is the individual explanation, followed by the general clarification.
As for the question "Why?", it is raised as a response to an inquiry:
since there are six enumerated items, why is there no characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?

The *tathatā* of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is called "freedom from desire," because it is manifested by being free from the desires of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).

It is said that one "skillfully enters" because one understands the essence of the mind through contemplation; it is called "constant" because there is no further entering or exiting; and it is called "pure" because it is free from the defilements of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*). This is precisely what was meant above by "not relying on the three realms."
Because it is spoken in accordance with reality, it is called "true speech"; because it skillfully guides others, it is called "expedient means.
Although it is effortless, it issues forth words in response to the capacities of beings, just like a celestial drum; this is what is meant by that.

All sentient beings possess only the single original enlightenment; by causing all beings to return together to this one awakening, it is said that benefiting others through this fundamental benefit is called the supramundane *dāna-pāramitā*.
The Sūtra says: "Supreme mindfulness is firm; the mind is always non-abiding; it is pure and unstained, unattached to the three realms—this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
The Commentary says:
Because one regards sentient beings with compassion as if looking upon an only son, it is called "supreme mindfulness is firm."
Because one constantly remains in the world without dwelling in nirvana, it is said that "the mind is eternally non-abiding.
This prevents the errors of the two vehicles.
Because the contemplation of the mind is luminously penetrating and unmixed with any outflows, it is said to be "pure and untainted."
Pervading the six realms of existence and realizing that they are all empty and quiescent, one is said to be unattached to the three realms.
This stops the evils of ordinary beings.

This clarifies that one does not dwell upon the characteristics of the precepts of either ordinary beings or sages; this is precisely what was previously called "not dwelling on the characteristics of the precepts," and it is named the supramundane *śīla-pāramitā*.

The Sūtra says: "Cultivating emptiness to sever the fetters while not relying on any forms of existence, and bringing the three karmas to stillness while not dwelling in body or mind—this is the pāramitā of kṣānti.
The Commentary says:

The first two phrases establish the principle of emptiness and depart from the fetters of existence; the latter two phrases quiet the three karmas and dissolve body and mind; all of these are the meaning of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
This refers to what was previously described as "purity and non-conceptuality.

The Sūtra says: "To be far removed from names and numbers, to sever the views of emptiness and existence, and to enter deeply into the emptiness of the aggregates (skandhas)—this is the *vīryapāramitā*."
The Commentary states:
The first two phrases signify the meaning of abandoning the coarse and attaining the refined; "entering emptiness" signifies the meaning of progress.
This is precisely what was stated above as "neither grasping nor releasing," which constitutes the supramundane perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

The Sūtra says: "To be fully detached from emptiness and stillness, yet not to abide in any forms of emptiness; for the mind to dwell in non-abiding within the Great Emptiness—this is the perfection of dhyāna.
The Commentary says:
"To be fully detached from emptiness and stillness" means that through skillful transformation, one takes birth throughout the three realms of existence.
"Not abiding in any emptinesses" means not being obstructed by the five types of emptiness, because one constantly transforms beings throughout the ten directions;
this clarifies the dhyāna of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
"The mind abides in non-existence" means that although the body engages with the three realms of existence, the mind always dwells in the principle of non-existence.
"Principle is non-existent" means that principle transcends the characteristics of the three realms of existence.
"Abiding in the Great Emptiness" means that although one constantly transforms beings throughout the ten directions, the mind remains within the Great Emptiness.
The "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā) is the emptiness of the great characteristics of the ten directions.
This reveals the accomplishment of the dhyāna of the Buddha-dharma.
Although the body engages in activity, the mind remains quiescent and unmoving; this is what was previously described as the nature [of mind] being equal to a vajra.
However, the meaning of "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā) briefly comprises five types:
first, the emptiness of both persons and phenomena is called Great Emptiness, as taught in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, and likewise stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Second, the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā* is called "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*), as taught in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and likewise stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
Third, the emptiness of the vessel world (bhājana-loka) is called "great emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*); as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the same is taught in the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*.
Fourth, the emptiness of the ālayavijñāna is called "great emptiness," as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*.
Fifth, the emptiness of the characteristics of the ten directions is called "great emptiness," as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This present scriptural passage occurs in the fifth [chapter], and is spoken here merely for the sake of convenience.

The Sūtra says: “The mind has no characteristics of mind; it does not grasp at empty space. Conditioned phenomena do not arise, nor is nirvāṇa realized. The mind has no coming or going, its nature being eternally equal. The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all dharmas is of a definitive nature; it does not rely on the stages (bhūmis), nor does it dwell in wisdom. This is the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Commentary states:
"The mind has no characteristic of mind" means that one does not maintain an internal contemplation of the mind's characteristics.
"Not grasping at space" means that one does not grasp at the emptiness of the mind's vacuity.
This is the wisdom of the realized path.
Regarding "all conditioned phenomena do not arise," it means one penetrates the fact that all conditioned phenomena are fundamentally non-arising.
Regarding "not realizing cessation," it means one does not cling to non-arising and constantly engages in the transformation of others.
This is the wisdom of the path of instruction.

Regarding "the mind has no entering or exiting and its nature is eternally equal": the two preceding paths are never separated from one another; it is moving yet ever-quiescent, and quiescent yet ever-moving, and thus there is no entering or exiting.
Movement and stillness are always concurrent and never stagnate in one extreme; therefore, their nature is eternally equal.

That all phenomena (*dharmas*) have the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as their definitive nature is an exposition of the mark of the eternal stillness of the path of realization, for this mark is identical to the ultimate reality and equal to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

"Not relying on the various stages and not dwelling in wisdom" refers to the reason for the constant movement of the teaching path: it is because one does not rely with attachment upon the tenfold Dharma-realm, nor dwell in stagnation within the wisdom of tranquil illumination.

Within this, it possesses the meanings of awakening-illumination, being a model for emulation, and the cessation of contention; that is to say, as mentioned above, it does not destroy the Three Jewels, and is thus called the supramundane *prajñāpāramitā*.
The preceding detailed explanation of the six perfections is concluded.
The Sūtra says: “Good son!
These six pāramitās all attain their fundamental benefit and enter into the nature of certainty; they transcend the world and are unimpeded liberation.”
The Commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which provides a general explanation.
This contains two parts:
First, it clarifies that the six perfections share the same liberation; subsequently, it reveals that liberation is itself nirvana.

Regarding the first point, the statement "all obtain the fundamental benefit and enter the nature of certainty" means that when the six perfections are first practiced, they are all identical to original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*), because original enlightenment manifests as the practice of fundamental benefit.
Entering the Tathāgatagarbha, its nature is fundamentally quiescent, without beginning or end, and because it is subject to no alteration or transformation.

Thus, by attaining the fundamental benefit through these six perfections, one remains far removed from the signs of deluded thought and saṃsāric flux; therefore, it is said that one "transcends the world."
Because one enters the dharma-nature, one pervades the dharma-realm; being signless, unconditioned, unbound, and unfreed, it is called "unimpeded liberation.
As the Sūtra says: "Good son!..."
Thus, the characteristics of the dharma of liberation are all characterized by signlessness and non-action; there is neither liberation nor non-liberation—this is called liberation. Why is this?
The characteristic of liberation is signless and without action; it is unmoving, undisturbed, quiescent, and nirvāṇa, yet it does not grasp at the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
The Commentary states:
This second section clarifies that liberation is precisely nirvāṇa.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, liberation is clarified, followed by nirvana.

Regarding the initial statement that "all practices are signless": the practices of the six pāramitās are identical to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Since the characteristic of original enlightenment is the detachment from characteristics and the detachment from nature, it is called "signless."
The practice of the six perfections is free from cultivation and free from action; therefore, it is called "non-action.
Since both the action and its characteristics are utterly extinguished, it is said that all are "characteristic-less practices.
Since the characteristics of the dharma of liberation are thus, how could there be a liberation that is separate from bondage?
What bondage could there be that is not liberated?
Therefore, it is said that there is neither liberation nor non-liberation.
As for the question "Why is this so?", why is it that the practice of the six perfections is called the practice of signlessness?
The answer to this is as follows:
These six perfections are not only liberation itself, but are also nirvana; therefore, they are said to be "practice without signs."
"The characteristic of liberation is signless and non-active" reiterates the aforementioned liberation.
"Immovable, undisturbed, and tranquil nirvāṇa" clarifies that this is indeed nirvāṇa.
To clarify that the practice of the six perfections as previously described is entirely without arousal and without distraction, it is itself primordial quiescence and nirvana.
Since it is indeed nirvana, how could there be any characteristics or practices?
Because it is free from the marks of agitation and turmoil, it is called "tranquil"; yet because it is also free from the nature of tranquility itself, one does not grasp at the mark of nirvāṇa.
Within this context, the six perfections, liberation, and nirvāṇa extend from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the stage of Buddhahood.
Regarding what is called "nirvāṇa," among the four types, it is precisely the originally pure nirvāṇa; it is the inconceivable liberation itself.
Because it possesses the sense of mastery and non-obstruction, it is therefore termed "unimpeded liberation."
Question:

The meaning of liberation is manifold; there is liberation within the double path, liberation within the three dots, liberation within the fivefold dharma-body, and liberation among the ten gates of liberation. Among these various gates, to which one does it belong?
Answer:
Among these three matters, it is liberation; for liberation is itself nirvana.

To manifest the practice of the six perfections and the virtues of these three matters, speaking in terms of actual attainment, they are already acquired from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, reaching ultimate perfection at the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).
As it is said in the sutra: "If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in the Great Nirvana, they are able to establish the great purpose," and so on, as explained at length.

The sutra says: Having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Vimukta was greatly delighted and attained what he had never experienced before; wishing to proclaim their meaning and intent, he spoke these verses:

"The Honored One of Perfect Great Enlightenment expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes; he teaches exclusively the One Vehicle, for there is no path of two vehicles—a single flavor, signless benefit."
"Just as the great void has nothing it does not contain, so according to their differing natures, all find their place within the fundamental state.
The Commentary says:
This is the second set of verses below.
Within this, the introductory sequence of the sūtra is presented first.
Among the seven verses of the formal stanzas, there are two parts:
the first six are individual verses, and the final one is a collective verse.
The beginning and middle also consist of two parts:
first, one verse and one line, which versify the preceding brief indication;
second, three verses and three lines, which versify the subsequent detailed explanation.
The brief summary states:

Because the ground of the Buddhas’ wisdom enters into the definitive nature of the true characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), all skillful means (*upāya*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are characterized by the benefit of signlessness (*animitta*). Now, among these verses, the first verse summarizes this point.

Furthermore, it is said that the definitive meaning of "one awakening" is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; yet for all sentient beings who can be saved, he teaches but a single flavor. Now, this verse expresses this through three meanings: the first line is the verse of the Dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā), the next two lines are the verse of the illustrative simile (dṛṣṭānta), and the final two lines are the verse of the application of the simile (upanaya).

The Sūtra says: "Just as that which is free from mind and self is accomplished by a single dharma, so too all beings, through their various similar and dissimilar practices, shall obtain their fundamental benefit and extinguish the dualistic views of subject and object."
The Commentary states:
From here below, the verses provide a detailed explanation of the text.
This section contains two parts:

The first five verses extensively explain the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*), while the latter two and a half verses extensively explain the meaning of single awakening (*eka-bodhi*).
Within the extensive explanation of signlessness, there is both a direct exposition and a further clarification.
Now, the first two lines of the verse provide a direct expansion of the prose.

Within that preceding direct expansion, there are also two parts: first, the contemplation of the preparatory means (*upāya*), and second, the elucidation of the actual contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
This present verse expands upon the text concerning the actual contemplation.
That statement, "causing those sentient beings to all be free from the self of mind," and so forth, extensively explains the distancing from subject and object;
these two lines now precisely versify that passage.

As for the term "one dharma," it refers to the Middle Way contemplation of oneness, which is free from the extremes of existence and non-existence, because by means of this one can abandon the grasping at a self of mind.
Within the text that further elucidates [the meaning], there are four question-and-answer exchanges; these two lines of verse now summarize the first two exchanges.
Regarding the phrase "those who practice the commonality and difference of all existences," it is stated in the answer to the first exchange:

"All mental characteristics are fundamentally without a basis," and so forth; such passages constitute the general characteristic contemplation (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*) of "common practice" (*samāna-caryā*).
In the second response, it is stated: "If there is a self, cause them to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination";

furthermore, it says: "If there is a self, cause them to eliminate the view of existence; if there is no self, cause them to eliminate the view of non-existence; if the mind arises, cause them to eliminate the nature of cessation; if the mind ceases, cause them to eliminate the nature of arising. Passages such as these constitute the contemplation of distinct characteristics through diverse practices.
Since there is no difference in what is entered through these identical and distinct practices, it is said that all obtain the fundamental benefit; as stated previously at the conclusion:
"To extinguish this seeing-nature is to enter the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
Furthermore, regarding this verse’s statement on "extinguishing the two views of appearance," it refers to the latter two rounds of question and answer.
In the third response therein, it says:
when seeing a phenomenon arise, one causes the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*) to cease; when seeing a phenomenon perish, one causes the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*) to cease.
Now, precisely to praise this, it is said that "the two views are extinguished.
The fourth response states:
"Both arising and ceasing are extinguished; what was originally born is not born. The mind is eternally empty and quiescent; being empty and quiescent, it has no abiding place."
Now, to precisely praise this, it is said that "the two marks are severed.
The Sūtra says: "The tranquil Nirvāṇa does not abide in the attainment of realization; it enters the state of certainty, being without marks and without activity."
The Commentary states:
The following two and a half verses extensively explain one awakening (*bodhi*).
Within this extensive explanation of one awakening, there is both a primary exposition and a further clarification.
In this present verse, only the reiterated exposition is versified.
Within this reiterated exposition, there are six questions and answers; here, two are presented:
the first verse versifies the sixth answer, and the subsequent one and a half verses versify the fifth answer. The preceding four questions and answers are omitted and not versified.
In the sixth response, it says:

"Entering the state of certainty, one transcends the world with unimpeded liberation; the characteristic of this liberation is signlessness, non-activity, immovability, and non-distraction—the tranquil nirvana—yet one does not even grasp at the characteristic of nirvana."
This verse here is presented in reverse order.

The Sūtra says: “The ground of the mind’s emptiness and quiescence, where the quiescent mind is unborn, shares the nature of that vajra, remaining indestructible within the Triple Gem; possessing the six pāramitās, it delivers all living beings.”
The Commentary states:
This is the fifth answer in verse.
That text says:

When the mind does not arise, there is no basis for support; the mind dwells in no conditioned phenomena, being eternally empty and quiescent, devoid of any differentiated marks. Furthermore, its nature is equal to the indestructible Three Jewels, as firm as a vajra; with an empty mind that is unmoving, one is endowed with the six pāramitās.
This verse here follows the sequence of the sūtra.
The sūtra says: “Transcending the three realms, none do so by means of the Hīnayāna; it is through the seal of the Dharma of the single flavor that the One Vehicle is accomplished.”
The Commentary states:
This single verse summarizes the general meaning of the preceding chapter.
