As for "that is both originally co-nonexistent and neither existent nor non-existent": those two [conditions] that could produce it are originally co-nonexistent; since there is no producer, it is not made to exist, hence it is called "not existent. Because it is not made to exist, there is no subsequent arising, hence it is said to be "non-existent."

Regarding the statement "if there is no arising, consciousness also does not exist": since the meaning of arising is absent, how could consciousness possibly exist? Because consciousness does not exist, the object does not arise from existence. Within this, there are two types of inference (*anumāna*): [1] the inference that because the effect is absent, the cause is absent; and [2] the inference that because the subject (*dharmin*) is non-existent, its attributes (*dharma*) cannot exist. Thus, it is established that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the Blessed One has said: "O monks, form is like a mass of foam; feeling is like a bubble; perception is like a mirage; formations are like a plantain trunk; and consciousness is like an illusion. This is what is meant by the statement: "If there is no arising, consciousness also does not exist. Furthermore, it is said: "The eye and forms are the conditions for the arising of eye-consciousness; the meeting of these three is contact; with contact as a condition, feeling arises; with feeling as a condition, craving arises; and so forth, until one fully understands suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation. This is what is meant by the statement: "If there is no arising, consciousness also does not exist. Moreover, it is said: "When the eye is intact and forms come into range, if there is no attention, eye-consciousness does not arise. When the eye is intact and forms come into range, if there is attention, eye-consciousness arises. This is what is meant by the statement: "If there is no arising, consciousness also does not exist. Furthermore, it is said: "When the eye is impaired and forms do not come into range, even if there is attention, eye-consciousness does not arise. When the eye is intact and forms come into range, and there is attention, eye-consciousness arises. This is what is meant by the statement: "If there is no arising, consciousness also does not exist. 2. Objects do not manifest, because they have no source, like [seeking] hair from a tortoise.
The preceding six sections on the analysis and resolution of doubts are concluded.
The Sūtra says: At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said, “The characteristics of dharmas are thus:

both internal and external are empty; the two categories of object and wisdom are fundamentally quiescent and extinguished. The true mark of ultimate emptiness spoken of by the Tathāgata—such a dharma is not an accumulation.”
The Commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which definitively establishes what has been taught.
It definitively determines that six [factors] are certainly neither diseases nor medicines.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, determining that it is not a disease; second, determining that it is medicine.
Within the first part, there are also two sub-sections:
Having examined and determined the admission,
the phrase "the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are thus" within the inquiry summarizes the previously explained sixfold characteristics of phenomena.
The mention of "internal and external" refers to the fact that consciousness takes both internal and external objects as its domain.
The term "two assemblies" refers to the multiplicity of objects and wisdom.

The term "non-accumulation" means that it does not accumulate the afflictions of the defilements of birth and death, nor does it accumulate various afflictions like those who wrongly grasp at emptiness.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “It is so.

The Dharma of suchness is without form and without abiding; it is neither that which is accumulated nor that which accumulates, neither meaning nor greatness—a single category of dharmas, a profound mass of merit.”
The Commentary states:
This is what the Tathāgata definitively allows.
He speaks of "formlessness" (ārūpya) because it prevents the affliction of giving rise to attachment to form.
"Non-abiding" is because it is also free from the affliction of wrongly grasping emptiness (*ayoniśaḥ-śūnyatā*).
"That which is not accumulated" is because the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is empty.
"That which does not accumulate" is because the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is empty.
"Non-meaning" refers to being free from the differentiated meanings of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth.
"Not great" refers to being free from the characteristics of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), such as earth, water, and the rest.

The "Dharma of the Single Root" refers to the One Original Enlightenment (*ekamūla-awakening*); taking this as its root, it is able to give rise to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and all meritorious qualities.
However, there are two categories:
first, the category of defilement, referring to the various fundamental consciousnesses, the meaning of which is as explained above;
second, the category of absolute purity, referring to the single original enlightenment, as explained in this text.
Within that fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), all seeds of defilement are accumulated;

within this fundamental awakening (*mūlapratyavekṣājñāna*), there exists only a mass of profound intrinsic qualities. It is called "profound" because it is free from characteristics and free from nature, and it is called a "mass" because its qualities exceed those of the sands of the Ganges.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, “The inconceivable and inconceivable assembly:

the seven and five do not arise; the eight and six are quiescent; the nine marks are empty and non-existent. Where there is emptiness, existence is non-existent; where there is non-existence, emptiness is non-existent.”

As the World-Honored One has taught, the meaning of all phenomena is empty; yet one enters this emptiness without ceasing activity, so as not to lose the continuity of karma. Being without self or what belongs to a self, the views of body and agent, object, and the internal and external fetters are all utterly stilled; thus, even aspiration comes to rest.

"In this way, the wisdom of principle-contemplation and the concentration on True Suchness—what the Venerable One constantly describes as being truly like the dharma of emptiness—is itself the excellent medicine.
The Commentary states:
"From here below is the second section, which definitively establishes that this is the medicine."
Within this, there are also two parts;
first, the Bodhisattva’s careful inquiry.
Within the inquiry, there are three sections:

First, summarizing the preceding accumulation of profound merit; second, mounting the manifest [vehicle] to enter deeply into the contemplation of principle; third, examining the excellent qualities of the sublime medicine.
Within the first section there are also three parts: a general heading, a detailed exposition, and a concluding summary.
The "Inconceivable Collection" is a general designation for the merits of being free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within its detailed exposition, it first clarifies the freedom from characteristics and subsequently reveals the freedom from intrinsic nature.

Regarding the statement at the beginning that "the seven and five do not arise," this is intended to clarify the emptiness of two types of derivative consciousnesses (*mūla-vijñāna*): the seventh is derivative within the ever-active consciousnesses (*nitya-pravṛtti*), while among the non-ever-active consciousnesses, the five sensory consciousnesses constitute the derivatives.

Regarding "the eighth and sixth are quiescent": this clarifies the quiescence of two types of fundamental consciousnesses (*mūlavijñāna*). Within the ever-active consciousnesses (*nitya-pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the eighth is the fundamental; within the non-ever-active consciousnesses (*anitya-pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the sixth is the fundamental. Thus, both are quiescent.
Next, the nature of detachment is revealed.
Regarding "the nine aspects being empty and non-existent": this is because even the aspect of the ninth consciousness does not maintain its own nature.

Regarding "emptiness existing and non-existence existing": this further establishes the characteristic of detachment, for the dharmas characterized by the existence of the eight consciousnesses are empty and non-existent.
"Neither emptiness nor existence" further establishes the nature of detachment; for the nine consciousnesses are empty and non-existent by virtue of their nature being signless.
When the single mind is thus detached from signs and detached from nature, it is itself a mass of immeasurable merit; this is what is called the "inconceivable mass."

Regarding the statement that "the meanings of the dharmas taught by the Honored One are all empty," this third section summarizes the departure from characteristics and the departure from intrinsic nature.
Next, the contemplation of principle is elucidated, which contains two parts:
a detailed exposition and a summary.
Within the separate elucidation, there are three phrases.
"Entering emptiness and non-action while not losing the various karmas" refers to the samādhi of emptiness.

This means that through the contemplation of principle one enters emptiness such that there is no action of subject and object; yet, although there is no subject or object, one does not lose the karma of the six perfections and so forth.
Next, the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) is explained.

Regarding the view of self, selfhood, the agent, and the object, this refers to being free from the signs of all afflictions associated with such views, because it is free from the signs of "self" and "mine," as well as the signs of the subject who sees and the object that is seen.

That all internal and external fetters (saṃyojana) and proclivities (anuśaya) are entirely stilled means that one is free from the characteristics of those fetters and proclivities belonging to craving; for the characteristics of the various fetters of the internal door, the various proclivities of the external door, and the afflictions (kleśa) of the three realms are empty.
This is called the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
As for "therefore even the vow ceases," this clarifies the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*):
because all phenomena of the three realms are quiescent, the mind that seeks through vows naturally and eternally ceases; this is called the wishless samādhi.
The phrase "Thus, the wisdom and concentration of principle-contemplation are true suchness" is a concluding statement.
As previously stated, all three are principle-contemplations; because there is no partiality between calming and insight, and no duality between subject and object.
Regarding the Venerable One’s frequent statement that the reality of the dharma of emptiness is itself a potent medicine, this is the third inquiry:
Since such a dharma of emptiness possesses all virtues and cures all fetters and afflictions, should it not therefore be considered a potent medicine?
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “It is so. Why is this?
Because it is empty:
emptiness is unborn, and the mind is eternally unborn; emptiness is unceasing, and the mind is eternally unceasing;
emptiness has no abiding, and the mind likewise has no abiding.
Emptiness is unconditioned, and the mind is likewise unconditioned.
Emptiness has no coming or going; it is free from all gain and loss, and the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all likewise non-existent.
The mind’s lack of attachment is also just like this.
“Bodhisattva!
I teach all forms of emptiness in order to dismantle all modes of existence.
The Treatise says:
This is the Tathāgata’s definitive authorization.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the general authorization.
Regarding the statement that "emptiness is the excellent medicine," it is precisely because of emptiness that existence gives rise to illness.
From the section on "the nature of emptiness" onwards is the second part, the specific concession.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies that by taking the medicine of emptiness, one is freed from the affliction of the fruit of saṃsāra;
second, it reveals that by taking the medicine of emptiness, one treats the illness of attachment to grasping.
Regarding the initial statement that "emptiness is non-arising and the mind is eternally non-arising": this is because the mind that enters emptiness is identical to emptiness in its non-arising;
furthermore, in accordance with non-extinction, the mind is eternally non-extinguished.
Arising and ceasing are precisely the meaning of impermanence; therefore, the opposites of those two are termed "permanent.

As for the mind also having no abiding, it is not only that it lacks the characteristics of beginning and end, but also that it lacks the characteristic of abiding in the middle; this specifically clarifies its separation from the three characteristics.
"The mind is also unconditioned" generally reveals its freedom from those three conditioned characteristics; this clarifies that by donning emptiness, one is free from the affliction of impermanence.
Next, it clarifies that one is also free from the affliction of grasping and attachment.
"Having no entering or exiting" means there is no distinction between exiting a contemplation and entering one.
"Being free from gain and loss" also means being free from the characteristics of acquiring something new or losing what was old.

"The mind not being attached is likewise" means that the observing mind is also like the principle of emptiness; it does not produce the characteristics of entering, exiting, gaining, or losing, nor does it become attached to phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense bases (*āyatana*). This clarifies that by donning emptiness, one leaves behind the maladies of grasping and attachment.
Regarding my statement that "I teach all emptinesses in order to shatter all existence," this is the third conclusion.

In terms of ultimate reality, the principle of emptiness is non-dual; yet, the teaching of the five types of emptiness and so forth is for the purpose of destroying the disease of those who cling to existence. Just as diseases are manifold, the teachings on emptiness are likewise taught accordingly.

Furthermore, in ultimate reality, it is neither empty nor non-empty; rather, emptiness is provisionally taught in order to refute [the notion of] existence. Within the statement "not empty," the nature of emptiness (śūnyatā) is not preserved as a substantial entity.
These two points summarize all teachings on emptiness.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, "Venerable One!
To know that existence is not real, like water in a mirage, and to know that reality is not non-existent, like the nature of fire, is this the wisdom of such a person?"
The Commentary states:
The six categories and six doubts were resolved in reverse order, with the specific resolutions and general determinations already concluded above.
Hereafter follows the second section, wherein one category and three doubts are eliminated in direct sequence.
Within this, there are three [sections]:
that is, within the single chapter on the *Tathāgatagarbha*, three doubts arise which are successively dispelled. The first doubt is as follows:

the verse by the householder Brahmacarin states, "If one says phenomena exist, it is like the delusion of water in a mirage"; and it further states, "If one sees phenomena as non-existent, it is like a blind man seeing no sun."
Based on that statement, some may give rise to doubt, asking:
"The householder is a worldly person; is such a judgment and explanation a false view, or is it true knowledge?"
Having raised such doubts, they are unwilling to believe or accept [the teaching].
To dispel those doubts, he cites that matter as a question.
The analogy of the mirage-water has already been explained as before.

"Knowing that reality is not non-existent" means being able to know that the nature of the single true meaning is not non-existent. Those who speak of those who reckon reality to be non-existent are like the blind who perceive the sun erroneously.

This "knowing that the elder knows reality is not non-existent" refers to the meaning of non-non-existence being like the nature of fire as a king. That is to say, it is like the element of fire within wood: though one may analyze and search for it, the characteristic of fire cannot be found; yet, the nature of fire within the wood is truly not non-existent, for if one drills and searches, the fire will certainly appear.

The single mind is also like this: although one analyzes its various characteristics and cannot find a "mind-nature," it is not that the mind within all phenomena does not actually exist; for when one cultivates the path and seeks it, the single mind becomes manifest.
In this way, the nature and characteristics of fire are concealed while its power is great, resembling that of a sovereign; therefore, it is called a "king.
Elder, is such an observation that avoids the two extremes considered wisdom?
Thus he asked.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “It is so.”

Why is this? Because this person practices true contemplation, contemplating the single state of quiescence; they grasp both the characterized and the uncharacterized equally through emptiness. By cultivating emptiness, they do not lose sight of the Buddha; by seeing the Buddha, they do not follow the three currents.
The Commentary states:
From here below, the Tathāgata resolves doubts.
This section contains two parts:
Direct decision and explanatory decision.
To say "it is thus" is to decide that this is wisdom.
As for the passage beginning with "Why is this?", it explains why this is wisdom.
Within this, there are two parts:
a brief explanation and a detailed exposition.
Regarding the first, the phrase "contemplating the single quiescence" refers to contemplating the meaning of the quiescence of the single dharma of mind.

Regarding "taking both the characterized and the uncharacterized as equal through emptiness": this means that when one contemplates the conventional world of characteristics and the ultimate truth of non-characteristics, they do not exist as separate entities because they are fused into one. Cultivating emptiness in this manner is in perfect accord with the Buddha-mind; therefore, one constantly beholds the Buddha-body.
Since he has never lost the opportune moment, it is said that he does not fail to see the Buddha.

Because his constant vision of the Buddha further increases his contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and as this contemplation of emptiness advances, it opposes all forms of existence (*bhava*); therefore, it is said that he does not follow the three currents.

The three floods (*ogha*) fully encompass the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms; namely, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
These are called the three floods, the meaning of which is as explained in the regular expositions.

The Sūtra says: "Within the Mahāyāna, the three paths of liberation are of one essence and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty (*śūnya*); because they are empty, they are signless (*animitta*); because they are signless, they are wishless (*apraṇihita*); because they are wishless, there is no seeking; because there is no seeking, there is no aspiration. By means of this activity, the mind is purified; because the mind is pure, one beholds the Buddha; and because one beholds the Buddha, one shall be born in the Pure Land."
“Bodhisattva!
By diligently practicing the three transformations within this profound Dharma and perfecting wisdom and concentration, one immediately transcends the triple world.
The Commentary says:
This is the second extensive exposition.
It contains two parts:
first, clarifying the benefits of the three paths of liberation; second, revealing the benefits of diligently practicing the three types of emanations.

Regarding the statement at the beginning that "the single essence is without intrinsic nature," this is said in contrast to the separate essences and intrinsic natures of the three gates of liberation in the Hīnayāna; it reveals that the contemplative practice of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas is a single essence.

When one contemplates the mind and realizes its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), three gates of liberation are established as provisional designations according to their respective meanings: the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*) is established in the sense of forgetting the essence and nature; the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*) is established in the sense of forgetting the essence and characteristics; and the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*), also called the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*), is established in the sense of forgetting the essence and function.

To manifest that there is only a single non-conceptual contemplation which, regarding the essence, characteristics, and functions of all phenomena, dispels nothing and integrates everything, the three gates of liberation are established.

Regarding "purifying the mind through these karmic actions": because one has forgotten all essence, characteristics, and functions, one is able to purify the mind that emerges from contemplation to engage with the mundane world, thereby becoming free from all defiled attachments. With a mind free from attachment, one is able to perceive the Reward Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*); by perceiving the Reward Buddha, one attains birth in the Pure Land. This constitutes the excellence of the path of the three liberations.
Regarding "thus diligently practicing the three transformations within the profound Dharma," this refers to diligently practicing the three types of emptiness within the Dharma of emptiness.

What are they? That the characteristic of emptiness is also empty is the first transformation-practice; that the emptiness of emptiness is also empty is the second transformation-practice; and that the object of emptiness is also empty is the third transformation-practice. Since their meaning is as previously explained, they are not discussed separately here.

By diligently practicing the three transformations, one immediately attains single-mindedness; because one attains single-mindedness, wisdom and concentration are perfected. The stage of such perfection transcends the three realms; this is the sublime benefit of diligently practicing the three transformations.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, "That which the Tathāgata has taught as neither arising nor ceasing is precisely impermanence.
Cessation is the cessation of arising; once arising and cessation have ceased, quiescent extinction is permanence. Because it is permanent, it is unceasing."

This is the dharma of non-interruption, which is free from all the moving and unmoving dharmas of the three realms; regarding conditioned dharmas as one would avoid a pit of fire, by relying on what dharma does one reproach oneself to enter that single gate?
The Commentary states:
The following section dispels the second doubt regarding the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter.
It says: "One clearly perceives that consciousness is eternal; this consciousness is eternally quiescent, and even that quiescence is itself quiescent."
Based on that text, some may give rise to doubt, asking:
"Although this eternally abiding dharma of quiescence is worthy of aspiration, it is subtle and profound.
The minds of sentient beings are coarse and shallow, difficult to discipline; how can they discipline their minds so as to enter that gateway?"
Driven by such doubts, he poses this question.
Within the question, there are two parts:
first, he points to the remoteness of the fruit; second, he asks about entering the cause.

Regarding the statement at the beginning that "non-arising and non-ceasing are themselves impermanence": this summarizes the preceding point that consciousness is eternally quiescent because it is originally quiescent.
Although it is without arising and without ceasing, it is not eternal by nature; therefore, it is impermanent.

Regarding the statement, "The cessation of this arising and ceasing—once arising and ceasing have ceased—is quiescent cessation and is eternal," this refers back to the previous point that even quiescent cessation is itself ceased.
Furthermore, it states that one clearly perceives consciousness as eternal.
From "Regarding conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛtadharma*) onwards, this is the second section: the formal inquiry into the skillful means for entering those gateways.
Although skillful means and correct contemplation were previously mentioned, they were explained only briefly; therefore, he requests a more extensive exposition.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “Bodhisattva!
One should rebuke one’s mind with respect to three great matters and enter into practice by means of three great truths.”
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said:
"In what way do the three matters reproach the mind?
In what way do the three truths enter into the single practice?"
The Buddha said:
"As for the three things: the first is called cause, the second is called fruit, and the third is called consciousness.
These three things are fundamentally empty and non-existent; they are neither the self nor a true self. Why, then, would you give rise to attachment and defilement toward them?"
Contemplating these three matters as being tossed about by fetters and drifting in the ocean of suffering, one should constantly reproach oneself for such conditions.
As for the three truths: first, the path to bodhi is the truth of equality, not the truth of inequality;
second, it is the truth attained through the right wisdom of great enlightenment, not the truth attained through false wisdom.
The third refers to entering the truths through the practice of non-differentiation between wisdom and concentration, rather than entering the truths through mixed practices.
By cultivating the path to Buddhahood through these three truths, there is no one who, within this Dharma, fails to attain perfect enlightenment.
"Attaining the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, one gives rise to the flow of supreme great compassion, benefiting both oneself and others, and attains the Bodhi of Buddhahood.
The Commentary states:
This passage consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the request; and fourth, the exposition.
The exposition consists of two parts:
first, the method for generating revulsion through criticism; second, the method for entering the path.
Regarding the first, "causes" refers to the causes of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
The "fruit" refers to the fruits of wealth and happiness among humans and devas.
The "consciousness" refers to that which can maintain cause and effect, namely the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Sentient beings conceive of this as their internal self, yet its nature is empty; therefore, it is not the self.
The principle of non-self is precisely the true self; therefore, one should not harbor attachment toward that which is not the self.

Regarding the observation of these three things as being drifted by fetters: this means that due to the four fetters, which obstruct the mind fixed upon the principle, these three things are caused to drift through the ocean of suffering.
What are called the four bonds (*yoga*)?

As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter on the Truths: "There are four kinds of bonds, namely: the bond of the body consisting of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-yoga*), the bond of the body consisting of ill-will (*vyāpāda-yoga*), the bond of the body consisting of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-yoga*), and the bond of the body consisting of the adherence to the view that 'this alone is the truth' (*tattvābhiniveśa-yoga*)."
They are called "fetters" because they obstruct the nature of the concentrated mind-body. Why is this?
It is because they obstruct the very essence of the concentrated mind; thus they are called fetters, not because they obstruct the physical body.
Why is this? Because they serve as the causes for four kinds of mental distraction. That is to say:

being caused by craving for wealth and possessions leads to mental distraction; being caused by improper conduct regarding matters of contention leads to mental distraction; being caused by the suffering of difficult vows and observances leads to mental distraction; and being caused by investigating objects through irrational means leads to mental distraction.

Because they rely on their respective individual views, they engage in various irrational speculations regarding objects of knowledge and give rise to false attachments, asserting: "Only this is true; all else is foolish and delusory."
With this as the cause, the mind becomes distracted.
Distracted toward what?
Toward the knowledge and vision of reality within the concentrated mind.
"One who constantly reproaches oneself for such matters does so because reproach can cast off the four bonds and because one grows weary of the three things from which one flows.
Having explained the method of reproach and weariness, what is the method of entry?
This refers to the thorough examination of the three truths.

First, regarding the statement that the path to bodhi is the truth of equality and not the truth of inequality: this means that the nature-pure bodhi realized by the Buddha is universally unobstructed and pervasive; therefore, it is called the "path."

All sentient beings share this same nature; there is not one who does not return to it. This is the ultimate path, and therefore it is said to be equal and not unequal. This is precisely the remedy for the separate inclinations of the two vehicles.

The second point means that the truth is attained through the correct wisdom of the Great Awakened One, not through false wisdom. This refers to the fact that the fruit of the Great Awakened One’s omniscience is attained solely by realizing equalizing correct wisdom; it is not attained through false wisdom that takes as its object such realms as the obscure *tattva* (ultimate reality) or the *mahat* (the Great One). This is precisely the antidote to the attachments of all non-Buddhist schools.

The third means that wisdom and concentration are without distinct modes of activity when entering the truths, rather than entering the truths through mixed modes of activity. This means that when one attains right knowledge and enters into equanimity, wisdom and concentration are perfectly integrated without separate characteristics; only then is this truly entering into the truth of equanimity.

It is not like the conceptual mind of the world, which treats the king and its attributes as distinct entities, or where concentration and wisdom function as separate practices; such mixed practice is not the true entry [into the path].
This refers to those who, as a remedy for worldly contemplative practices, have not yet realized [the truth] but claim they have, thereby falling into the pride of overestimation (*abhimāna*).
These three types are collectively termed "truths" (*satya*) because they are the objects of observation for the contemplation of thorough investigation.

By universally counteracting these three kinds of divergent attachments, one is able to correctly cultivate the single Buddha-way; therefore, it is said that one cultivates the Buddha-way by means of these three truths.
Next, the fruit obtained through the cultivation of the path is revealed.

The statement that "there is no one who does not attain perfect enlightenment regarding these dharmas" reveals the fruit of the wisdom and virtue of self-benefit; for by cultivating the Buddha-way within these three dharmas, there is none who fails to obtain the fruit of perfect enlightenment.

"Attaining the flow of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment and the great ultimate compassion" reveals the fruit of the merit of benefiting others; for it universally flows as the great ultimate non-referential compassion, pervading the entire dharma realm so that there is nothing not benefited.

"Benefiting both oneself and others to achieve the Bodhi of Buddhahood" summarizes the preceding two points, as it refers to the attainment of Equal Enlightenment through the perfection of the two benefits.
The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said, "O Venerable One!"
"Such a dharma is without causes and conditions; if there are no conditions for a dharma, its cause does not arise. How then can an immovable dharma enter the Tathāgata?
The Commentary states:
The following section dispels the third doubt concerning the "Tathāgata-garbha" chapter.
As stated at the end of the verses in that chapter: "The transformation of the grasped and the grasper enters the Tathāgatagarbha. Based on this, some may raise a doubt, saying:

"If the path to enlightenment and the truth of equality herein are themselves the Tathāgatagarbha, independent of the power of causes and conditions, how can one transform the causes of the grasped and the grasper and thereby enter the dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha?"
There may be those who harbor such doubts; therefore, I shall address their inquiry.

As for "being without causes and conditions," it is because of equality that one does not arise from causes and conditions, and because of equality that there are no other conditions. Since other conditions are absent, causes cannot be activated. How then can one enter the state of the Tathāgata by employing causes and conditions within that which is devoid of the dharma of activation?
If that which enters by the power of causes were to depend upon conditions, it would not be immovable.
The Sūtra says: At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The characteristics of all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and immovable; these phenomena do not arise at this time, nor do they arise at any other time."
Dharmas have no time of difference; they do not arise at a different time. Dharmas have neither motion nor non-motion; because their nature is empty, they are quiescent.

At the time when their nature is empty and quiescent, this dharma manifests at that very time. Because it is free from marks, it dwells in stillness; because it dwells in stillness, it does not take objects as conditions.
The Commentary states:
From here below, the Tathāgata definitively resolves their doubts, proclaiming the meaning of how one may enter into that which is equal, immovable, yet accessible.
Within these eight lines of verse, there are two parts:
The first three [verses] provide a brief exposition, while the latter five offer a detailed proclamation.
Within the brief exposition, there are two parts:
the first three verses clarify the meaning of immovability, and the final verse clarifies the meaning of attaining entry.

The beginning and middle consist of three parts: the thesis, the explanation, and the conclusion. Specifically, the first two lines present the thesis regarding the meaning of immovability, while the following four lines provide the explanation of that meaning of immovability.

Regarding the statement that "this dharma does not arise at this time": "this time" refers to this world; this world is the present. The present moment never abides even for an instant; once the subtle [past] and the yet-to-be [future] are removed, there is no intermediate state. Just as when one removes the passing of light and shadow, there is no intervening space, so too, at such a time, arising cannot occur.

Regarding the statement that "dharmas have no time of difference, nor do they arise at a different time": what is called "a different time" refers to the past and the future. Since the future does not yet exist, it lacks the sense of arising; since the past has already ceased to exist, it likewise lacks the sense of arising. By this principle, dharmas possess no movement or arising.
Since there is neither the movement of arising nor the immobility of abiding, it is said that phenomena are without movement;
because their nature is empty of movement and non-movement, they are quiescent. These two phrases conclude the meaning of non-movement.
Next, there is one verse that clarifies the meaning of "attaining entry.

Regarding the phrase "at the time when nature is empty and quiescent": it means that at the moment one clearly perceives that nature is empty and quiescent, the unmoving Dharma manifests; because it manifests within the mind, it is said that one has "attained entry."
Thus, the first half clarifies the meaning of "entering.

Now, this reveals that the Dharma is free from all marks; because it is free from all marks, it abides in tranquility; because it abides in tranquility, it never arises from conditions. Therefore, although there is "entry," it does not abandon the meaning of being free from conditions.
Thus, the latter half [of the verse] clarifies the meaning of being free from conditions.

The Sūtra says: "These dharmas of dependent origination—these dharmas do not arise through conditions; since causes and conditions have no arising or ceasing, the nature of arising and ceasing is empty and quiescent."

The capacity for conditions to serve as objects of perception is the fundamental principle of dependent origination; therefore, phenomena do not arise from conditions, and likewise, conditions do not arise.

Phenomena produced by causes and conditions are themselves the causes and conditions; yet the characteristics of arising and ceasing within those causes and conditions are themselves devoid of arising and ceasing.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the second section, the detailed exposition.
Within this, there are two parts:
The first three verses extensively explain the meaning of immovability, while the latter two verses proclaim the meaning of attaining entry.

Within the former group, there are also two parts: the first two verses demonstrate immovability by tracing back to the non-attainment of the root, and the final verse demonstrates immovability by following through to the non-attainment of the branches.
The beginning consists of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.

The initial statement, "These dharmas of dependent origination are dharmas that do not arise through conditions," is the heading, which indicates that these resultant dharmas do not arise from conditions.
Next, there are four phrases explaining the meaning of non-arising.

"The arising and ceasing of causes and conditions are non-existent" clarifies that because all causes and conditions arise and cease without abiding, they lack the functional capacity to produce an effect.

Regarding "the nature of arising and ceasing is empty and quiescent": because it does not abide, there is neither arising nor ceasing; because its nature is empty and quiescent, it likewise does not produce results.

Regarding "the nature of conditions as the object and the subject of cognition": the seeds of causal conditions lying latent are called "nature" (*svabhāva*); the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), being the faculties that can confront objects, is called the "subject of cognition" (*ālambaka*); the objects of cognition, being what the faculties confront, are called the "object of cognition" (*ālambana*; the *samanantara-pratyaya*, or condition of immediate succession, is not discussed here as it involves the cessation of dharmas).

Thus, because the nature of the seed-condition, as well as its two aspects—the subjective and the objective—both arise from the fundamental condition, it is said that these conditions arise from the fundamental condition.
This is its very basis; the various conditions are also as previously explained. Because the nature of arising and ceasing is empty, there is no functional activity of arising.
By means of these three points, the meaning of the non-arising of conditions is established.
Therefore, regarding "the arising of dharmas is not from conditions": this means that the arising of resultant dharmas is not produced by conditions.
Regarding "the non-arising of conditions is likewise": this means that the non-arising of conditions is the same as their result.
Next, there is one verse which, by pursuing the secondary, reveals the immovable.

The statement "Dharmas produced by causes and conditions are themselves dharmas that are causes and conditions" clarifies that all resultant dharmas also function as causes and conditions, because they act as conditions in relation to subsequently arising dharmas.

Since these resultant phenomena already function as causes and conditions, they are identical to what was previously explained regarding the emptiness of the nature of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is said that although the characteristics of arising and ceasing exist through causes and conditions, they are themselves devoid of arising and ceasing.

Previously, when explaining in brief, the emptiness of the fruit was directly revealed; now, in this extensive explanation, it is discussed in terms of causes and conditions. This is intended to reveal that the immutability of the cause and effect of all phenomena is itself the path of equal enlightenment, and that enlightenment is not to be sought elsewhere outside of these phenomena.
This is the general purport of this verse.
As Master Zhao said:
"Is the Way far away?"
In every encounter with phenomena, there is the Real.
How distant can the Sage be?
To embody this is itself the Divine.
The Sūtra says: “That which is like the true mark does not, from the beginning, arise or cease. At this time, all phenomena spontaneously undergo arising and ceasing.

Therefore, the ultimate purity is primordial; it is not produced by the power of various conditions. It is precisely within the subsequently attained state that one attains what was originally attained.”
The commentary states:
These two verses proclaim the meaning of "attaining entry.
Within this, there are three parts:
First, one verse shows that amidst all movement, the Tathāgata is revealed as being unmoving;
second, two lines clarify that this immovability is fundamentally independent of manifold conditions;
third, two lines clarify the meaning of attaining entry by means of dharmas that are themselves free from conditions.
Regarding "the place obtained subsequently," this refers to the place obtained after the Path.
In the previous brief explanation, the phrase "at the time of cessation" (*nirvāṇa-kāla*) is precisely what is meant here by "the place obtained subsequently.
Since it is already cessation, how could there be a place or a time?
It is merely because [the original attainment] is separated from time and place that it is provisionally designated by means of time and place.

Regarding "attainment upon attainment within the original attainment": initial awakening (ādikṣaya) is called "attainment" because it is ultimate; it is so named because it is that which is capable of attaining.
Ultimate initial awakening is identical to original awakening; for this reason, it is said that one attains what was originally attained.
This concludes the third section, "Resolving Doubts. The Sūtra says:

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha heard what the Buddha had taught, his mind was filled with joy. Then, among the assembly, there were none who harbored any doubt. Having understood the minds of the multitude, he spoke these verses:
"I knew the doubts in the minds of the assembly, which is why I questioned so earnestly and firmly.
The Tathāgata, in his great kindness and compassion, has distinguished all things without exception.
Thus, both these assemblies have attained complete clarity."

Now, within the sphere of realization, I universally transform all sentient beings; like the great compassion of the Buddha, I do not abandon my original vow, and thus I abide amidst the afflictions on the stage of the only son.
The Commentary states:
This is the fourth comprehension.
Within these three verses, there are two parts:

The first one and a half verses conclude the preceding section on the benefits of resolving doubts, while the latter one and a half verses set forth the subsequent practice of universal transformation.

Regarding the "Stage of the Only Son" (*ekaputraka-bhūmi*): from the first bhūmi upward, one has already realized the equality of all sentient beings and regards all beings as one looks upon an only son. This is called the pure *adhyāśaya* (resolute intention); it is metaphorically designated as the "Stage of the Only Son" to express this state of mind.
As for abiding within afflictions, although the bodhisattva has attained the equality of all dharmas, he does not abandon afflictions by means of his power of skillful means.
If he were to abandon all latent tendencies of affliction, he would immediately enter nirvana, thereby contravening his original vow.

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the section on the Determination of Samāhita: "The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) should be said to be untainted (*anāsrava*), because it is dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*), because it is not associated with them, because it lacks an object of cognition (*ālambana*), and because it is not produced by any of the afflictions."
Because this supramundane state cannot be practiced by any ordinary beings, except for those bodhisattvas who have already entered the distant stages (*dūrabhūmi*).

Although such bodhisattvas are able to give rise to supramundane dharmas so that they manifest before them, they do not abandon their afflictions due to the power of their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
The commentary states:
Regarding the term "not relinquishing" used here, it does not mean a final relinquishment such as that of an Arhat and so forth; therefore, it is called "not relinquishing.
Yet, it is not a case of total non-relinquishment; thus, it is said to be "not relinquishing."
The details therein are as explained in the chapter on the two obstructions (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).

Because they do not abandon [the afflictions], it is said that they "dwell in the afflictions"; because of this, they do not enter nirvāṇa, but rather universally transform the realms of the ten directions.
Within this one-fascicle sutra, the second part—the main exposition—has already concluded above.
The sutra says: At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the assembly, saying:
"This bodhisattva is inconceivable; he constantly uproots the suffering of sentient beings through great compassion."

If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra-dharma and uphold the names of these bodhisattvas, they shall not fall into the evil realms, and all obstacles and difficulties will be entirely eliminated.

If there are sentient beings who, free from all other distracting thoughts, single-mindedly recite this sutra and practice it according to the Dharma, at that time the Bodhisattva will constantly manifest transformation bodies to preach the Dharma for them. He will protect these people, never abandoning them for even a moment, and cause them to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the third part, titled the "Distribution" (Pravartana).
Within this, there are six sections:

First, circulation through praising others; second, circulation through exhorting the assembly; third, circulation through establishing names; fourth, circulation through upholding and maintaining; fifth, circulation through repentance; sixth, circulation through practice and observance.
This constitutes the first praise for the person who disseminates [the teaching], praising those capable of circulating this sutra.
There are four kinds of supreme virtues of a Bodhisattva:

first, the virtue of universally transforming all beings through great compassion; second, the virtue of specifically benefiting those who uphold this sutra; third, the virtue of manifesting transformation bodies to preach the Dharma; and fourth, the virtue of causing others to attain the ultimate fruit.
The Sūtra says: "O Bodhisattvas, if you transform sentient beings, cause them all to practice such a Mahāyāna of definitive meaning.
The Commentary says:
This is the second exhortation for the assembly to circulate [the teaching].
"Definitive and ultimate" means that it reveals the most profound and supreme [teaching], such that nothing further can be added.
The Sūtra says: At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"The mass of merit of the Mahāyāna spoken by the Tathāgata definitively severs the fetters; its benefit of the realization of non-arising is inconceivable."
What is the name of this Dharma teaching?
How much merit is obtained by receiving and upholding this sutra?
I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will explain this for me.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the third section, establishing the title for circulation, which first poses a question and subsequently provides an answer.
Within the question, there are also two parts:
First one accepts [the teaching], and subsequently one inquires about it.
Within the act of acceptance, four kinds of superior capacities of this sutra are revealed:
first, it enables the holder to obtain immeasurable merit, as the sutra states, "the mass of merit of the Mahāyāna."
Second, it enables the holder to eternally sever all fetters, as the sūtra says, "definitively severing the fetters";
third, the intended meaning it conveys is the benefit of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), as the sūtra says, "the benefit of the realization of non-arising";
fourth, the teaching that expresses it is difficult to fathom, as the sūtra says, "inconceivable."
In the subsequent questions, two matters are addressed:
first, the question regarding the title of the sutra, for the purpose of knowing its essential meaning;
second, the question regarding the merit of upholding it, because one seeks merit by upholding the sutra.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “Good son!
As for the name of this sūtra, it is ‘The Inconceivable Protection and Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the Past,’ and it enables one to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing wisdom.”

If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra, they will have nothing further to seek among all other sutras; for the Dharma of this sutra is a dhāraṇī that encompasses all teachings, subsuming the essentials of all sutras and serving as the fundamental tenet of the Dharma of all sutras.
Regarding the names of this sutra: it is called the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-sūtra*, also called the *Vajrasamādhi*, and also called the *Amitārthasiddhānta*.
The Commentary states:
From here below, there are two parts in the response, as they answer the two questions respectively.
The introduction also has two parts:
first, praising the meaning of the name; second, formally establishing the name.
The first of these also has two parts:
First, there is a general praise of the name; second, there is a specific elucidation of its meaning.
From the phrase "Able to enter" (*neng ru*) onwards is the specific elucidation of the meaning, which reveals three points.
The passage from "Able to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom" up to "having no further aspirations" elucidates the meaning of the name of the Vajrasamādhi.

There is no dharma that cannot be destroyed and no principle that is not exhausted; by means of this, one is led to enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, for beyond this there is nothing further to be hoped for.
This scripture’s Dharma is the dhāraṇī of all dharmas and the compendium of the essentials of all sūtras; this reveals the name and meaning of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding the phrase "the fundamental tenets that bind these various sūtra teachings," this refers to the meaning of the name "the tenet of immeasurable meanings.
What is the distinction between these two names and their respective meanings?
The preceding section clarified the meaning of how [this treatise] extensively subsumes the various sūtras, while the subsequent section revealed the ultimate tenet upon which those sūtras rely.
Regarding the detailed explanation of the three names established therein, it has already been expounded at length within the first two gates of the text.

The Sūtra says: "If there is anyone who receives and upholds this sūtra, they are said to receive and uphold the merits of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Just as space is boundless and inconceivable, so too is this; that which I entrust to you is solely this sūtra."
The Commentary states:
This is the answer to the second question.
Within it, four kinds of supreme virtues are revealed:
First is the supreme quality of upholding the Buddhas, because this sutra can encompass the minds of all Buddhas, as the sutra says, "upholding the names of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas";
second is the supreme quality of vastness, because the sutra says, "it has no boundaries or limits";
third is the supreme quality of profundity, because the sutra says, "it is inconceivable."
Fourth is the incomparable, supreme excellence, as the sutra states: "It is solely this scripture.
The sutra says: Ānanda asked:
"What is the mental practice?"
"How is it that a person upholds this sutra?
The Buddha said, "Good son!

Those who receive and uphold this sutra have minds free from gain or loss; they constantly cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Even amidst frivolous discourse, they always delight in a pure mind; when entering a village, their minds remain in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and even while living as householders, they do not cling to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
The Commentary states:
From here below is the fourth section, on receiving, upholding, and disseminating [the teaching], which contains two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of receiving and upholding; second, the further elucidation through dialogue.
The beginning and middle also consist of two parts:
first the question, and second the answer.
Within the question, there are two parts:
First, he asks about the mental conduct of those who uphold the sutra; second, he asks about the benefits and merit of those who uphold the sutra.
In the response, these two questions are answered in sequence.
Regarding the first, five kinds of mental conduct are clarified:
First, being single-mindedly free from gain or loss, because one does not observe the long or short [faults] of others;
second, constantly practicing pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), because one internally cultivates pure conduct that is free from signs;
third, always delighting in a tranquil mind, because one remains unmoved amidst movement.
Fourth, their minds are constantly in meditative concentration because they enter into states of distraction without being scattered;
fifth, they do not cling to the three realms of existence because they dwell within defilement without being stained by it.
The Sūtra says: "This person possesses five kinds of merit in the present life:"

First, being respected by the multitude; second, not meeting with untimely death; third, being able to provide skillful responses to heterodox arguments; fourth, delighting in delivering sentient beings; and fifth, being able to enter the noble path.
"Such a person as this upholds this sutra.
The Commentary states:
This answers the second question; by following the preceding five lines, one obtains these five blessings.
That he is respected by the multitude is because he does not observe the long or short [faults] of others.
That his body does not meet with untimely death is because he constantly cultivates practice free from signs (*animitta*).
One who refutes erroneous doctrines does so because they delight in a tranquil mind.
One who delights in delivering sentient beings does so because they enter into the samādhi that is both dispersed and constant.
One who is able to enter the noble path does so because they do not cling to the three realms of existence.
The Sūtra says: Ānanda said, "If that person were to deliver all sentient beings, would he be worthy of receiving offerings?
The Buddha said:

“Such a person as this can serve as a great field of merit for sentient beings; constantly practicing great wisdom, they manifest both the provisional and the ultimate. They are the Saṃgha of the Four Reliances, and they may accept all offerings—even one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain—let alone robes and food.”
“Good son! Such a person as this is your spiritual friend and your bridge; how much more so should you make offerings to ordinary beings?
The Commentary says:
The following section provides a detailed exposition through a series of exchanges.
It contains two parts:
first, the clarification of the nature of the field of merit; second, the revelation of its capacity to generate merit.
This is the first [of the four reliances].
Regarding the four reliances upon the Saṃgha: the first reliance refers to those possessing the nature of afflictions, whose stage is prior to the bhūmis;
the remaining three reliances refer to those on the bhūmis, as explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: Ānanda said, “If one receives and upholds this sūtra from that person, and makes offerings to that person, how much merit will be obtained?
The Buddha said:

"Furthermore, if there were someone who took gold and silver filling an entire city and gave it as a gift, it would not be equal to one who receives and upholds even a single four-line verse of this sutra from such a person and makes offerings to that person."
The Commentary states:
This is the second [point] clarifying that those who uphold the sūtra can generate vast merit.

Even if one were to bestow gold and silver filling an entire city as a gift upon those who do not uphold the sūtra, the merit obtained would not equal the merit gained from providing a single meal or a single garment as an offering to one who upholds even this four-line verse.
The Sūtra says: “Good son!
Those sentient beings who uphold this sūtra shall have their minds constantly in samādhi and never lose their original mind.
If they should lose their original mind, they must immediately perform repentance; the method of repentance is that which brings cooling relief.”
The Commentary states:
From here below is the fifth section, on Repentance and Circulation.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, the merit of repentance is praised; second, it is further elucidated through a dialogue.

Regarding the first point, "cool" (*śītala*) means "clear" because it extinguishes the turbidity of unwholesome causes, and "cool" because it is free from the feverish affliction of the fruits of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The Sūtra says: Ānanda said, “To repent of prior transgressions is not to enter into the past.
The Buddha said:
"It is so. Just as in a dark room, when one encounters a bright lamp, the darkness is immediately extinguished. Good son!
It does not say that one repents all previous transgressions, but rather states that one enters the past.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the second section, which further clarifies through a series of exchanges.
Within this, there are two rounds of question and answer:
the first round clarifies the principle of repentance, while the second round clarifies the ritual method of repentance.
Here, the intent of the question is as follows: regarding the statement that one repents prior transgressions, does it not follow that those prior transgressions have already entered the past?
If that which was previously non-existent now enters the past, how could there be repentance for what is without fault?
In the answer, it says "it is thus": because such prior faults do not enter the past, there is no repentance for what is non-existent.

Why is this so? Because the sins previously committed perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and their seeds flow continuously in the present; by this principle, they have not yet entered the past.
Furthermore, when confession is able to treat [the offense] at the time it arises, it prevents those seeds of transgression from manifesting in the present.
This is like how the darkness in a room is extinguished precisely when a lamp is lit.
Because the seeds of transgression do not reach the present, it is only at that time that they are said to enter the past.

Regarding the absence of a confession for previously committed sins: that which was previously committed cannot be reached by confession, because it is impossible to cause that which was not previously there to become so;
however, what was previously committed can be prevented from manifesting in the present, and this non-manifestation is brought about by the act of confession.

The difference between this and the meaning of severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is as follows: the former concerns the path of arising and ceasing, whereby that which has not yet arisen is prevented from reaching the present;
the latter concerns the path of continuity, whereby that which previously existed is prevented from reaching the present.

Furthermore, one who severs the fetters (saṃyojana) permanently eradicates the seeds; one who repents past transgressions impairs and subdues the potent functioning of those seeds so that they do not manifest in the present. It is on the basis of this principle that it is said [the fetters] have entered the past.
The Sūtra says: Ānanda asked, "What is meant by 'repentance'?
The Buddha said:

"By relying on the teachings of this sutra to enter the contemplation of reality, at the very moment one enters this contemplation, all transgressions are completely extinguished; one departs from the evil realms and shall be reborn in a Pure Land, swiftly attaining Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
The Commentary states:
This is the second method for the practice of repentance.
The response consists of two parts:
First the practice is clarified, and subsequently the benefits are shown.

Regarding the initial section, the statement "entering the contemplation of reality by relying on the teachings of this sutra" means that by relying on the principles of the Vajrasamādhi, one destroys the characteristics of all phenomena; this is called entering reality. This is the semblance of true contemplation prior to the [first] bhūmi.

Regarding "when one enters contemplation, all transgressions are completely extinguished": all karmic obstacles of transgression arise from false conceptualization. Now, by breaking through all marks and entering true contemplation, one suddenly shatters all realms of false conceptualization; therefore, all transgressions are simultaneously and entirely extinguished.
Next, the benefits are revealed, which consist of two phrases.
"Departing from all evil realms and being born in a pure land" clarifies the provisional retribution (*puṇya-phala*).
"Swiftly attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" demonstrates the ultimate retribution (*vipāka-phala*).

The Sūtra says: When the Buddha had finished preaching this sūtra, Ānanda, the various bodhisattvas, and the fourfold assembly were all greatly rejoiced; their minds attained certainty, and they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joyfully receiving and practicing his teachings.
The Commentary states:
This is the sixth section, concerning the practice and dissemination [of the teaching].
Within it, there are four phrases.
"All were greatly rejoiced" means they rejoiced upon hearing the Dharma.
"Their minds attained certainty" means they were freed from all doubts and delusions.
"They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet" means they revered the Dharma and honored the person.
Those who joyfully practice find increasing delight as they proceed.

Now, having relied upon and placed my faith in these profound and subtle Vajra teachings, I have briefly recorded them; may this root of virtue pervade the entire Dharma-realm, universally benefiting all beings without exception.

Vajrasamādhi Sūtra Śāstra, Volume II. May the precious reign be boundless and the imperial court be filled with auspicious joy; may all disturbances and dust of strife forever subside, and the court and the commonalty enjoy peace and prosperity. May the Duke of Jinyang’s ocean of merit deepen further, and his mountain of longevity rise as high as the heavens.
Next, I pray that my widowed parents and Fo-nu may transform their groans into songs and enjoy long lives; I shall have this printed on wooden blocks and distributed as offerings.

Furthermore, reflecting that this sutra originated from the Dragon Palace and its inception was prompted by illness, I further vow that it shall reach all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, so that in every birth they may never hear the sound of sickness and, never dwelling within a womb, may always roam through the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas.
Recorded by the Upāsaka Zheng Yan on the fifth day of the eighth month in the year Jiachen.
